lessons.plain: Cloud computing means renting computing power, storage, networking and software over the internet from a provider such as Microsoft Azure, instead of buying and running your own machines. You use what you need and the provider runs the buildings and hardware. Think of renting a flat instead of owning a house. The landlord fixes the roof and the plumbing, but you lock your own door and look after your belongings. The shared responsibility model is that tenancy agreement for the cloud. It sets out which security and upkeep jobs belong to the provider and which stay with you, the customer.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company moves its customer database onto Azure, and an employee's password is stolen and used to download the data. Whose job was it to protect that account: Microsoft's or your company's? Make a guess and give your reason.
lessons.teach:
Cloud computing is the delivery of computing services over the internet on demand. Those services include servers, storage, databases, networking and software. A provider owns and operates the physical datacenters, and customers rent capacity instead of buying hardware. A datacenter is a building full of servers, power and cooling.

The shared responsibility model divides the security and maintenance work between provider and customer. It works because each party protects what it actually controls. The provider controls the physical layer: the datacenter building, the physical network cables and switches, and the physical servers (called hosts). The provider is always responsible for those. The customer controls who logs in and what gets stored. So the customer is always responsible for its data, its devices (the laptops and phones people use to connect), and its accounts and identities, meaning the user names, passwords and permissions.

The layers in between are the operating system, the network settings and the applications. Who looks after them depends on how much of the service the provider runs for you. The more the provider manages, the more of that middle work moves to the provider.

Worked example. A shop rents a virtual machine in Azure, which is a software-based computer that runs on Microsoft's hardware, and installs its own database on it. Step 1: a disk fails in the datacenter. Microsoft replaces it, because physical hardware is the provider's job. Step 2: a security patch is released for the operating system on the virtual machine. The shop must apply it, because the shop chose and controls that operating system. Step 3: an employee shares an admin password. That is the shop's problem, because accounts are always the customer's job.

Common mistake: assuming that moving to the cloud means the provider secures everything. In a running system, this belief leads to unpatched servers, storage left open to the public, and weak passwords. Any of these can expose data while the provider's own infrastructure keeps working perfectly. Responsibility for data and identities never transfers to the provider.

questions.prompt: A design studio rents two virtual machines in Azure to run its 3D rendering software. A virtual machine is a software-based computer that runs on the provider's hardware. Step 1: a cooling unit in the datacenter breaks, and Microsoft repairs it, because the physical building and its equipment are the provider's job. Step 2: the maker of the rendering software releases a security fix, and the studio installs it, because the studio chose and controls the applications on its own virtual machines. Step 3: a designer's laptop, which she uses to connect to the virtual machines, gets infected with malware. Who is responsible for dealing with the infected laptop, and why?
choices: Microsoft, because the laptop connects to virtual machines that run on Microsoft's hardware.
Microsoft, because any security problem in a cloud setup is handled by the provider.
The studio, because the devices people use to connect are always the customer's responsibility.
Both parties share it equally, because a laptop is one of the middle layers, like the operating system.
questions.why: Devices such as the laptops and phones people use to connect are always the customer's job, no matter how much of the service the provider runs.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm is deciding whether to move to the cloud. Which description best matches what cloud computing means?
choices: Installing accounting software on each employee's laptop so that no network is needed.
Handing the provider every security task, including the firm's passwords and its client files.
Renting computing services such as servers, storage and databases over the internet, on demand, from a provider that runs the datacenters.
Buying new servers and installing them in a room at the firm's own office.
questions.why: Cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of computing services over the internet, with the provider owning the hardware and the customer renting capacity instead of buying it.

questions.prompt: A logistics company currently runs a virtual machine and patches its operating system itself. It switches to an Azure service where Microsoft runs much more of the platform for it. How does the shared responsibility split change?
choices: The company becomes responsible for the physical servers (hosts), because it now uses more of Microsoft's platform.
Work such as operating system upkeep moves toward Microsoft, but data, devices and accounts stay with the company.
Everything moves to Microsoft, including the company's data and user accounts.
Nothing changes, because responsibility is fixed no matter which service is used.
questions.why: The more the provider manages, the more of the middle layers it takes over, but data, devices and identities never transfer to the provider.

questions.prompt: A charity stores its donor records in Azure storage and accidentally leaves that storage open to the public. The records leak, even though Microsoft's datacenters, network and servers all keep working normally. What best explains this outcome?
choices: Microsoft failed in its duty, because storage sits in its datacenters and is therefore fully its responsibility.
The fault belongs to whichever party manages the operating system on the storage.
The charity assumed the provider secures everything, but protecting its own data is always the customer's responsibility.
This cannot happen, because data stays safe as long as the provider's infrastructure is working.
questions.why: Data is always the customer's responsibility, so a customer can expose its data through its own settings even while the provider's infrastructure works perfectly.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says, "We're moving to Azure, so security is Microsoft's problem now." In your own words, explain what cloud computing is and how the shared responsibility model splits the work. Name one thing that never moves to the provider, and explain why the split is not the same for every service.
lessons.modelAnswer: Cloud computing means we rent servers, storage, networking and software over the internet from a provider like Azure instead of owning the hardware. That does not hand all the security work to Microsoft. Under the shared responsibility model, Microsoft always covers the physical side: the datacenters, the physical network and the host machines. We always keep our data, the devices our staff use, and our accounts and identities. If someone steals one of our passwords and downloads data, that is on us. The middle layers, such as the operating system, network settings and applications, depend on how much of the service Microsoft manages. If we rent a virtual machine, we patch its operating system ourselves. With a more fully managed service, Microsoft takes on more of that work. The tradeoff is that handing over more work usually means we get less control over how those layers are set up.
rubricPoints: Defines cloud computing as renting computing services on demand over the internet instead of owning hardware.
States that the provider is always responsible for physical datacenters, the physical network and the hosts.
States that the customer always keeps responsibility for data, devices, and accounts or identities.
Explains that the middle layers (operating system, network settings, applications) shift depending on how much the provider manages.
Names a tradeoff or limit, such as less control when the provider manages more, or customer misconfiguration still exposing data.

suggested.rationale: This objective is about understanding a definition and a division of duties well enough to correct a teammate's misconception, so explaining it back in your own words is the core skill to practise.

lessons.plain: A cloud model describes who owns the computers your systems run on and who else shares them. In a public cloud, a provider such as Microsoft Azure owns huge data centers and rents computing power to many customers over the internet. In a private cloud, the computing resources serve one organization only, usually in buildings it controls. A hybrid cloud connects the two so work and data can move between them. Think of housing. Public cloud is renting a flat in a big building. Private cloud is owning your own house. Hybrid is keeping your house but renting extra rooms when relatives visit.
lessons.guessPrompt: A hospital must keep patient records on hardware it controls, but its public appointment-booking website gets very busy every January. Would you put everything in one place, or split it? Where would each part go, and why?
lessons.teach:
A public cloud is computing capacity (servers, storage, networking) owned and run by a provider and shared by many customers, called tenants. You reach it over the internet, buy no hardware, and pay only for what you use. You can add capacity in minutes, but you have less physical control over where and how the hardware runs.

A private cloud is computing capacity used by a single organization. It usually runs on-premises, meaning in a data center the organization owns or controls, though a third party can host it. You get full control over hardware, location and configuration. The tradeoff is that you buy and maintain the equipment up front, and your capacity is limited to what you bought.

A hybrid cloud combines a public and a private cloud and connects them, so applications and data can move or work across both. It lets you keep tightly controlled workloads private while using public capacity for everything else or for temporary peaks. This is sometimes called bursting.

Worked example: a retailer has two needs. Step 1: a regulation says payment records must stay on hardware the company controls. Control is the deciding requirement, so those records go in a private cloud. Step 2: the online shop gets five times its normal traffic for three weeks each December. Buying servers for that peak would leave them idle the rest of the year, so the shop runs in the public cloud and scales up only when needed. Step 3: the shop must check payment records, so the two environments are connected. That makes the overall design hybrid.

A common mistake is assuming private automatically means more secure. Security depends on how well the systems are run, and a private cloud makes you responsible for all of it. Another is calling the use of two public providers hybrid. That is multi-cloud.

In a running system, a poor fit is costly. A spiky workload in a private cloud either runs out of capacity during a surge or wastes money on idle hardware the rest of the year.

questions.prompt: A regional hospital is choosing where to run two workloads. Step 1: a privacy rule says patient scan images must stay on hardware the hospital controls. Control is the deciding requirement, so the images go in a private cloud, meaning computing capacity used only by the hospital, here in its own data center. Step 2 is MISSING: the hospital's research team runs large statistical jobs on anonymized data for two days at the end of each month, needing about 40 extra servers only during those two days. Decide where these jobs run and why. Step 3: the research jobs must read summary figures from the private environment, so the two environments are connected, which makes the overall design hybrid. Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: Buy 40 more servers for the hospital data center, because owning the hardware gives full control over the monthly jobs.
Run the jobs with a second public provider as well, because using two providers is what makes the design hybrid.
Run the jobs in the private cloud, because keeping everything on hospital hardware makes all workloads automatically more secure.
Run the jobs in a public cloud, because capacity can be added for the two days and paid for only while it is used.
questions.why: The jobs are a short, repeating peak with no on-premises control requirement, so pay-as-you-go public capacity avoids buying 40 servers that would sit idle about 28 days a month.

questions.prompt: A design firm runs its file storage with one public cloud provider and its rendering jobs with a different public cloud provider. It has no data center of its own. Which term correctly describes this setup?
choices: Multi-cloud, because it uses more than one public provider
Private cloud, because each provider holds only the firm's own files
Public cloud bursting, because rendering uses extra capacity
Hybrid cloud, because two separate environments are connected
questions.why: Hybrid means combining a public and a private cloud; using two public providers with no private cloud is multi-cloud.

questions.prompt: A two-person startup has no money to buy servers and cannot predict whether its new app will have 100 users or 100,000 next month. Which cloud model fits best, and why?
choices: Hybrid cloud, because every new app should keep part of its data on-premises
Public cloud, because it needs no hardware purchase and capacity can be added in minutes
Private cloud hosted by a third party, because that removes the up-front equipment cost
Private cloud, because full control over hardware protects the app as it grows
questions.why: The startup has no control requirement but needs no up-front cost and fast, usage-based scaling, which is what a public cloud provides.

questions.prompt: An accounting firm runs its tax-filing portal only in its own private cloud, sized for normal monthly traffic. During the six-week tax season, traffic jumps to eight times normal. What is the most likely problem, based on how a private cloud works?
choices: The firm pays the provider for idle shared servers, because private cloud billing is usage-based
The portal runs out of capacity during the surge, because capacity is limited to the hardware the firm bought
Nothing, because a private cloud scales up automatically like a public cloud
The portal becomes multi-cloud, because extra traffic is spread across providers
questions.why: A private cloud's capacity is limited to purchased hardware, so a spiky workload sized for average traffic runs short during the peak, while sizing for the peak would waste money the rest of the year.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between public, private, and hybrid cloud, and give one situation where each fits. Include one limitation or tradeoff of the private cloud.
lessons.modelAnswer: The difference is who owns the hardware and who shares it. In a public cloud, a provider like Azure owns the hardware and many customers share it. We rent capacity over the internet, pay for what we use, and can scale in minutes. That suits something like a new website with unpredictable traffic. A private cloud is used by our organization alone, usually in our own data center. That suits data a regulation says must stay on hardware we control. The tradeoff is that we buy the equipment up front, maintain it ourselves, and are stuck with the capacity we bought, so a sudden surge can overwhelm it. A hybrid cloud connects the two. We could keep sensitive records private and run the busy customer-facing parts in public cloud, bursting there during peaks. Private is not automatically more secure. It just means we carry all the security work ourselves.
rubricPoints: Defines public cloud as provider-owned capacity shared by many tenants and rented over the internet on a pay-per-use basis.
Defines private cloud as capacity dedicated to one organization, usually on-premises, with full control.
Defines hybrid cloud as public and private connected so workloads and data can work across both.
Matches each model to a situation using a stated requirement such as control, regulation, or variable demand.
Names a private cloud tradeoff such as up-front cost, ongoing maintenance, or fixed capacity.
Avoids treating private as automatically more secure, or confusing hybrid with multi-cloud.

suggested.rationale: The skill this objective tests is reading a scenario's control, regulation, and demand requirements and justifying a model choice, which exam-style situations practise better than any current mission.

lessons.plain: Consumption-based pricing, often called pay-as-you-go, means you pay the cloud provider only for what you actually use, measured in small units such as hours of computing or gigabytes stored, and billed afterwards. There is no big upfront purchase and no long contract. It works like an electricity meter: lights on, the meter runs; lights off, it stops. The alternatives trade flexibility for a lower price. You can promise to use something for a year or more in exchange for a discount, or accept cheap spare capacity that the provider can take back at short notice.
lessons.guessPrompt: A test server is needed for about two hours a day, while a production database must run every hour of every day for the next three years. Which of the two would you expect to benefit from paying only for the hours used, and which from committing to a long contract for a discount?
lessons.teach:
Consumption-based pricing (pay-as-you-go) is a pricing model where a provider meters your usage, such as compute hours or storage gigabytes, and bills you for exactly that amount afterwards, with no upfront payment and no commitment. It turns computing into an operational expense (OpEx), meaning an ongoing running cost, instead of a capital expense (CapEx), meaning a large upfront purchase of hardware you own.

It works because the provider pools huge amounts of hardware across many customers, so it can rent small slices by the hour and absorb the risk of idle machines. You gain flexibility: scale up, scale down, or stop, and the bill follows.

Other models trade that flexibility for price. A reservation (in Azure, a reserved instance) is a commitment, typically one or three years, to a resource in return for a large discount; you pay whether or not you use it. Spot pricing sells the provider's spare capacity very cheaply, but your workload can be evicted, meaning stopped, when the provider needs it back.

Worked example, in fictional credits. A virtual machine costs 0.10 credits per hour pay-as-you-go. A one-year reservation brings it to 0.06 per hour, charged for all 730 hours in a month. A dev server used 8 hours a day for 22 days runs 176 hours: 176 times 0.10 is 17.6 credits pay-as-you-go, versus 730 times 0.06, or 43.8 credits, reserved. Pay-as-you-go wins. A server running all month costs 730 times 0.10, or 73 credits, pay-as-you-go versus 43.8 reserved. The reservation wins.

A common mistake is assuming pay-as-you-go is always cheapest. It is the most flexible, not the lowest rate; for steady, always-on work it costs the most. The opposite mistake matters in a running system too: forgetting to stop unused pay-as-you-go resources means the meter keeps running, and idle machines quietly fill the bill. Match the model to the usage pattern: variable or short-lived work suits pay-as-you-go, steady predictable work suits reservations, and interruptible work suits spot.

questions.prompt: A small online shop runs a reporting database server. Pay-as-you-go costs 0.20 credits per hour. A one-year reservation costs 0.12 credits per hour and is charged for all 730 hours in a month. The server only runs during a monthly reporting push, 300 hours in total. Step 1: Pay-as-you-go cost is 300 times 0.20, which is 60 credits. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: Choose the cheaper model for this usage pattern. Which choice correctly completes Step 2 and the decision?
choices: Reserved cost is 730 times 0.12, which is 87.6 credits, so pay-as-you-go is cheaper.
The reservation has the lower hourly rate, so it is cheaper whatever the hours.
Reserved cost is 300 times 0.12, which is 36 credits, so the reservation is cheaper.
Reserved cost is 730 times 0.20, which is 146 credits, so pay-as-you-go is cheaper.
questions.why: A reservation is billed at its discounted rate for every hour of the month whether used or not, so 730 times 0.12 is 87.6 credits, which is more than the 60 credits pay-as-you-go costs for 300 hours.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes consumption-based (pay-as-you-go) cloud pricing?
choices: Your usage is metered and you are billed afterwards for exactly what you used, with no upfront payment or commitment.
You pay a large upfront amount for hardware you own, which counts as a capital expense.
You buy the provider's spare capacity cheaply, accepting that it may be taken back.
You commit to a resource for one or three years in exchange for a large discount.
questions.why: Pay-as-you-go meters actual usage and bills for it afterwards with no upfront cost or commitment, making it an operational expense; the other options describe CapEx, reservations, and spot pricing.

questions.prompt: An animation studio renders video frames overnight. If a render job is stopped partway, it can simply be restarted later with no harm, and the studio's main goal is the lowest possible price. Which pricing model fits best?
choices: Pay-as-you-go, because it is always the cheapest option
Buying their own servers as a capital expense
A three-year reservation, because it gives the deepest discount
Spot pricing, because the work can tolerate being evicted
questions.why: Spot pricing sells spare capacity very cheaply, and its risk of eviction does not matter for interruptible work that can be restarted.

questions.prompt: A team creates several test virtual machines on pay-as-you-go pricing, then leaves them running untouched during a two-week holiday. What happens to their bill?
choices: Nothing is charged, because pay-as-you-go only bills for machines doing useful work.
The charges are converted into a discounted reservation automatically.
The provider evicts the machines because they are idle, ending the charges.
The meter keeps running, so they are charged for all those idle hours.
questions.why: Pay-as-you-go bills for metered running time, not useful work, so forgotten idle resources keep adding to the bill until someone stops them.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what consumption-based pricing is and when you would choose it over a reservation or spot pricing, naming one limit or tradeoff of pay-as-you-go.
lessons.modelAnswer: Consumption-based or pay-as-you-go pricing means the provider meters what we use, like VM hours or storage, and bills us for just that afterwards. No upfront hardware purchase, no contract, so it is an operating expense rather than a capital one. It is ideal when usage is unpredictable, short-lived, or experimental, because we can stop resources and stop paying. The tradeoff is that it has the highest per-hour rate. If something runs all day every day for years, a one- or three-year reservation gives a big discount, though we pay even if we stop using it. Spot capacity is cheapest of all but can be taken back at short notice, so it only fits work that can be interrupted and resumed. The other risk with pay-as-you-go is forgetting idle resources, which keep billing until someone shuts them down.
rubricPoints: Defines pay-as-you-go as metered billing for actual usage with no upfront cost or commitment.
Links it to operational expense rather than capital expense.
Explains that reservations trade a commitment for a discount and suit steady workloads.
Explains that spot pricing is cheap but can be evicted, so it suits interruptible work.
Names a limit of pay-as-you-go, such as the highest unit rate or paying for forgotten idle resources.

suggested.rationale: Pricing a workload in fictional credits under pay-as-you-go, reserved, and spot models lets the learner see the break-even point directly instead of memorising it.

lessons.plain: Serverless computing is a way of running code where you hand the cloud provider a small piece of code and say when it should run, and the provider handles everything underneath: finding a machine, starting it, adding more when demand rises, and shutting it off afterward. You pay only while your code is actually working. Servers still exist, but you never see, size, or patch them. Think of a taxi instead of owning a car: you don't buy, insure, or park anything. You just ride when you need to and pay for the trip.
lessons.guessPrompt: A small online shop needs to resize product photos, but uploads only happen a few times a day. Would you rather keep a server running all day waiting for uploads, or pay only for the seconds spent resizing? What might you give up with the second option?
lessons.teach:
Serverless computing is a cloud model where the provider runs your code on demand and fully manages the machines, operating system, and scaling. You supply only the code and the rules for when it runs. Two Azure examples: Azure Functions, a managed service that runs short pieces of code, and Azure Logic Apps, a managed workflow service where you link steps together, often with little or no code.

Three ideas define it. Event-driven means code runs in response to a trigger, which is the event that starts it, such as a file upload, an incoming web request, a queue message, or a timer. Automatic scaling means the provider starts more copies when many events arrive and scales to zero, meaning nothing is running, when none do. Pay-per-execution means you are billed for the number of runs and the time and memory each one uses, not for idle hours. This works because the provider shares a huge pool of machines among many customers and assigns capacity only for the moments it is needed.

Worked example: a shop owner uploads a photo. Step 1, the upload is the trigger. Step 2, the provider finds capacity and starts the resize function. Step 3, the function runs for about two seconds and saves a smaller image. Step 4, the provider releases the capacity. Step 5, the bill reflects two seconds of work. If 500 photos arrive at once, the provider runs many copies in parallel without anyone adding servers.

A common mistake is believing serverless means no servers at all. Servers exist; you just do not manage them. A second mistake is assuming it suits every workload. Serverless is a form of platform as a service focused on short, event-triggered tasks. For a steady, always-busy, long-running job, paying per execution can cost more than a fixed server, and runs may have time limits. After idle periods, the first request can be slower while capacity starts up, which is called a cold start.

questions.prompt: A city library uses Azure Functions, a managed service that runs short pieces of code, to email reminders about overdue books. The function's trigger (the event that starts it) is a timer set for 06:00 each day. Trace one day. Step 1: at 06:00 the timer fires, and this is the trigger. Step 2: the provider finds spare capacity and starts the reminder function. Step 3: the function runs for about four seconds and sends 120 reminder emails. Step 4: the provider releases the capacity, so nothing is running (scaled to zero) for the rest of the day. Step 5: ??? Which statement correctly completes Step 5?
choices: The library pays nothing at all, because serverless means no servers were used to run the code.
The bill reflects about four seconds of run time and the memory used during that single run.
The library's IT staff shut down the server they started for the job so that billing stops.
The library is billed for 24 hours of a reserved server, because the function must stay ready for tomorrow's timer.
questions.why: Pay-per-execution billing charges for the number of runs and the time and memory each run uses, not for idle hours, so one four-second run is what gets billed.

questions.prompt: A colleague at a travel agency says: 'If we move our booking checks to serverless computing, our code will run without any servers.' Which statement correctly describes serverless computing?
choices: Servers exist, but your team must patch their operating system and add more when traffic grows.
Servers still run the code, but the provider manages the machines, operating system, and scaling for you.
There are truly no servers; the code runs directly inside the provider's network cables.
Servers exist only in your own building, and the cloud simply sends events to them.
questions.why: Serverless does not remove servers; it means the provider fully manages them, their operating system, and scaling while you supply only the code and the rules for when it runs.

questions.prompt: A logistics company is choosing which of its tasks to move to serverless computing, where code runs on demand in response to events and is billed per execution (per run, by time and memory used). Which task is the poorest fit?
choices: Encoding video continuously at full load around the clock, with each job running for hours.
Checking each new order message whenever one lands in a queue, a few times per hour.
Building a short sales summary on a timer once each night, taking about one minute.
Reading a scanned invoice whenever a driver uploads one from the road.
questions.why: A steady, always-busy, long-running job can cost more per execution than a fixed server and may hit run time limits, whereas the others are short, event-triggered tasks that suit serverless.

questions.prompt: A concert-ticket website runs its search code on Azure Functions, a managed service that runs short pieces of code. No one uses the site overnight. At 07:00 the first visitor's search takes several seconds longer than usual, but searches after that are fast. What best explains the slow first request?
choices: A cold start: after scaling to zero overnight, the provider had to start capacity before the first run.
The trigger failed on the first event, so the visitor's request was retried automatically.
Pay-per-execution billing deliberately slows the first request each day to reduce cost.
The function reached its run time limit overnight and the provider restarted it at 07:00.
questions.why: After idle periods a serverless function scales to zero, so the first request waits while the provider starts capacity, which is called a cold start.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what serverless computing means and when you would pick it, including at least one limit or tradeoff that could make it the wrong choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: Serverless means we write a small piece of code, tell the cloud what event should start it, and the provider handles the machines, patching, and scaling. Servers still exist, but we never manage them. It is event-driven: an upload, an HTTP request, a queue message, or a timer triggers the code. It scales out automatically when many events arrive and down to zero when nothing is happening, and we pay per execution instead of for idle time. In Azure, that is Azure Functions for code and Logic Apps for workflows. I would pick it for bursty or occasional work, like resizing images or processing orders. The tradeoffs: for a constantly busy, long-running workload, per-execution billing can cost more than a fixed server; runs can have time limits; and after idle periods the first request may be slow because of a cold start.
rubricPoints: States that the provider manages servers, operating system, and scaling while the customer supplies only code.
Explains that code runs in response to triggers or events.
Mentions automatic scaling, including scaling to zero when idle.
Describes paying per execution rather than for idle capacity.
Clarifies that servers still exist, they are just not managed by the customer.
Names a limit such as cost for steady workloads, time limits, or cold starts.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests whether you can spot when a scenario's bursty, event-driven, pay-only-when-used requirements point to serverless, so reasoning through realistic situations builds that judgment best.

lessons.plain: High availability means a service keeps working even when some part of it breaks, so users rarely notice an outage. Scalability means a service can handle more (or less) work by adding (or removing) computing power. Think of a supermarket. Having several tills open means one broken till doesn't stop shoppers paying. That is availability. Opening extra tills when the queue grows on a Saturday, then closing them on a quiet Tuesday, is scalability. In the cloud, the provider has huge pools of hardware in many locations, so you can get both without buying and wiring the spare tills yourself.
lessons.guessPrompt: A shop's website runs on one server. On Black Friday it slows to a crawl, and on another day the server's power supply dies. Which of those two problems is about handling more work, and which is about staying up when something fails?
lessons.teach:
High availability is a system's ability to stay usable even when individual parts fail. It works through redundancy, which means running extra copies of a component so another copy can take over. In Azure you can place copies in separate datacenters within a region (Azure calls these availability zones) so a power or cooling failure in one building does not take you down. Providers state their uptime commitment in a service-level agreement (SLA). An SLA is a written promise of a minimum uptime percentage, usually with service credits if the provider misses it.

Worked example: take a 30-day month, which is 43,200 minutes. An SLA of 99.9% allows 0.1% downtime, so 43,200 x 0.001 = 43.2 minutes a month. At 99.99% the allowance is 43,200 x 0.0001 = 4.32 minutes. Each extra nine cuts the allowed downtime by a factor of ten, and it usually costs more because you pay for more redundant copies.

Scalability is the ability to change capacity to match demand. Vertical scaling, or scaling up, gives one machine more CPU or memory. Horizontal scaling, or scaling out, adds more machines that share the work. Elasticity means capacity grows and shrinks automatically as load changes, often called autoscaling. Because cloud billing is by consumption, scaling back down saves money, and you avoid buying hardware sized for your busiest day.

A common mistake is treating the two ideas as the same thing. Scaling one server up to a bigger size adds capacity, but it is still one server. If it fails, the service is down. Scaling out across zones can give you both capacity and availability.

In a running system, skipping redundancy turns a single hardware fault into a full outage. Skipping scaling turns a traffic surge into slow pages and timeouts. Either way, customers are hurt even though nothing is wrong with your code.

questions.prompt: A concert-ticketing company runs its booking site on a service whose SLA promises 99.95% uptime. The operations lead wants to know how much downtime that allows in one 7-day week. Step 1: A week has 7 x 24 x 60 = 10,080 minutes. Step 2: [missing] Step 3: Multiply the week's minutes by that decimal: 10,080 x 0.0005 = 5.04 minutes of allowed downtime per week. Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: The allowed downtime is 100% minus 99.95%, which is 0.05%, written as the decimal 0.005
The allowed downtime is 100% minus 99.95%, which is 0.05%, written as the decimal 0.0005
Use the uptime figure as a decimal, 99.95% = 0.9995, because the SLA is stated as uptime
The allowed downtime is 0.05%, so multiply by 0.05 directly
questions.why: The downtime share is whatever the SLA does not promise (0.05%), and to use a percentage as a multiplier you divide it by 100, giving 0.0005, which yields the 5.04 minutes in Step 3.

questions.prompt: An online florist gets about ten times its normal traffic in the week before Valentine's Day, then traffic drops back. The owner wants capacity to grow automatically during the rush and shrink afterward so the bill falls when demand falls. Which idea matches this requirement?
choices: Placing copies of the site in separate availability zones
Elasticity, also called autoscaling
Choosing a service with a higher SLA percentage
Scaling up once to the largest machine size and leaving it there all year
questions.why: Elasticity means capacity grows and shrinks automatically with load, and because cloud billing is by consumption, shrinking after the rush lowers cost.

questions.prompt: A small medical clinic moved its booking system onto one very large virtual machine with lots of CPU and memory, believing this made the system highly available. A hardware fault later stopped that machine and bookings went down completely. What was the flaw in their thinking?
choices: Scaling up added capacity but it was still a single machine, so there was no redundant copy to take over
The provider's SLA guarantees that no outage can occur, so the provider broke the contract
They should have scaled down to cut costs, which also improves availability
The machine was too small, so scaling up further would have prevented the outage
questions.why: Vertical scaling makes one machine bigger but adds no redundancy, and without an extra copy a single hardware fault becomes a full outage.

questions.prompt: A payroll company is choosing between two tiers of a service: one with a 99.9% SLA and one with a 99.99% SLA. Which statement about the two tiers is correct?
choices: The 99.99% tier allows one tenth as much downtime and usually costs more, since it relies on more redundant copies
The 99.99% tier allows more downtime because it has one more digit
The 99.99% tier usually costs less because fewer failures happen
The 99.99% tier removes the need for redundant copies across availability zones
questions.why: Each extra nine cuts the allowed downtime by a factor of ten, and that higher commitment is usually paid for through more redundant copies.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between high availability and scalability in the cloud, and describe one tradeoff or limit of each, using an SLA percentage or a scaling choice as your example.
lessons.modelAnswer: High availability is about staying up when something breaks. You get it through redundancy: extra copies of a component, ideally in separate datacenters such as availability zones, so another copy takes over. The provider's SLA states the promised uptime. 99.9% allows about 43 minutes of downtime in a 30-day month, while 99.99% allows about 4 minutes. The tradeoff is cost, because more nines means paying for more redundant copies. Scalability is about matching capacity to demand. Scaling up makes one machine bigger. Scaling out adds more machines, and elasticity does that automatically and shrinks back down so you only pay for what you use. A limit of scaling up is that you eventually hit the largest machine size, and you still have a single point of failure. So scaling up adds capacity without adding availability. Scaling out across zones can give you both.
rubricPoints: Defines high availability as staying usable despite component failures, achieved through redundancy.
Explains that an SLA is a stated uptime promise and translates a percentage into allowed downtime.
Distinguishes vertical scaling (bigger machine) from horizontal scaling (more machines).
Describes elasticity as automatic scaling up and down so you pay only for the capacity you use.
Names a tradeoff, such as higher cost for more nines or a single point of failure when only scaling up.

suggested.rationale: The unit is mastered by reasoning through scenarios, such as picking redundancy versus scale-out and converting SLA percentages into downtime against a stated requirement, more than by memorising definitions.

lessons.plain: Reliability is a system's ability to keep working, or recover quickly, when something breaks, such as a failed server, a power cut or a flooded building. Predictability is being able to trust in advance how the system will behave: steady speed for users, and spending you can forecast. In the cloud, a big provider like Microsoft Azure runs many buildings full of computers around the world, so your app can be copied to more than one place and a failure in one spot need not take you down. Think of a delivery company with several depots. If one depot closes, parcels route through another, and the company can still quote delivery times and prices.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company's website runs on one server in one office closet. If you moved it to a cloud provider that has buildings in many cities, what could happen differently on the day that office loses power?
lessons.teach:
Reliability means a workload, meaning an application and the resources it runs on, can recover from failures and keep doing its job. Predictability means you can confidently forecast two things: performance, which is how fast and responsive the system is for users, and cost, which is how much you will spend.

Why the cloud helps reliability: Azure is built from datacenters, which are buildings full of servers, grouped into regions, which are geographic areas. Because this infrastructure is spread worldwide, you can place copies of your workload in separate locations. That redundancy, meaning spare copies ready to take over, lets the workload survive the loss of one location.

Why the cloud helps predictability: for performance, features like autoscaling, which automatically adds or removes computing power as demand changes, and load balancing, which spreads incoming requests across several servers, keep response times steady during busy periods. For cost, you can estimate spending before you build with a pricing calculator, track it as you go, and set budget alerts that warn you before you overspend.

Worked example. A ticket-selling site runs copies in two Azure regions. Step 1: a storm cuts power to a datacenter in the first region. Step 2: the copy there stops answering. Step 3: traffic is sent to the copy in the second region. Step 4: customers keep buying tickets with little disruption. That is reliability. Meanwhile, a concert goes on sale and traffic triples; autoscaling adds servers so pages stay fast, and the finance team, who set a monthly budget alert, sees the forecast rise and is not surprised by the bill. That is predictability.

Common mistake: assuming the cloud makes you reliable automatically. The provider supplies the global building blocks, but if you place your only copy in one location, a failure there still takes you offline. Another mistake is thinking predictable cost means a fixed price; under pay-for-what-you-use billing, cost varies but can be estimated and monitored. In a running system, ignoring either leads to outages or surprise bills.

questions.prompt:
A regional clinic runs its online appointment-booking app on Azure. Trace what happens.

Step 1: To save effort, the team deploys the app's only copy to a single datacenter in one Azure region.
Step 2: A cooling system failure forces that datacenter to shut down its servers for six hours.
Step 3: ???
Step 4: The team realises they relied on the cloud to be reliable for them. They plan to add a second copy in another region so one location can take over if the other fails.

Which statement correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Patients cannot book appointments, because no spare copy exists elsewhere to take over.
A budget alert warns the team, and the app recovers once the alert is acknowledged.
Azure moves the app to another region on its own, since cloud apps are reliable by default.
Autoscaling adds servers in the same datacenter, so booking keeps working normally.
questions.why: Reliability comes from redundancy that you set up yourself, so with only one copy in one location, a failure there takes the app offline.

questions.prompt: In cloud computing, what two things does predictability let you confidently forecast?
choices: Uptime and recovery time after a failure
Performance and cost
Security and compliance
The number of regions and datacenters you will use
questions.why: Predictability means forecasting performance, which is how fast and responsive the system is, and cost, which is how much you will spend.

questions.prompt: A payroll software company is moving to Azure with pay-for-what-you-use billing. Its finance lead says: 'Our spending will go up and down. I just need to know roughly what it will be and get warned before we overspend.' Which approach best meets this requirement?
choices: Turn on load balancing so requests spread across several servers
Estimate costs with a pricing calculator, track spending, and set budget alerts
Run copies of the app in two regions so spending is shared between them
Negotiate a fixed monthly price so the bill never changes
questions.why: Cost predictability in the cloud comes from estimating before you build, monitoring as you go, and setting budget alerts. You do not need a fixed price for this.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's Azure bill went from 4,200 dollars one month to 5,100 dollars the next after a busy shipping season. Their budget alert had already shown the forecast rising. A manager says, 'The bill changed, so the cloud is not predictable.' What is the best correction?
choices: Predictable cost does not mean a fixed price; it means the varying cost could be estimated and monitored, as the alert showed.
The manager is right; predictable cost means the bill stays exactly the same every month.
The bill changed because the firm lacked a copy in a second region, which is a reliability problem.
Predictability only refers to performance, so the cost change is not relevant to it.
questions.why: Under pay-for-what-you-use billing, cost varies but stays predictable when it can be estimated and tracked, and the budget alert forecast the rise.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how moving a workload to the cloud can make it more reliable and more predictable, and name one limit or tradeoff that means these benefits are not automatic.
lessons.modelAnswer: Reliability is about recovering from failures and carrying on. Azure has datacenters grouped into regions across the world, so we can run copies of our app in more than one place. If one location loses power, another copy keeps serving users. Predictability has two sides. Performance predictability comes from autoscaling, which adds computing power when demand rises, and load balancing, which spreads requests across servers, so users get steady response times. Cost predictability comes from estimating spend upfront with a pricing calculator, tracking it, and setting budget alerts. The limit is that none of this happens just because we are in the cloud. If we deploy only one copy in one region, a failure there still takes us down. Extra copies also cost more money, so we trade some cost for resilience. And pay-as-you-go cost is forecastable, not fixed, so we still have to watch it.
rubricPoints: Defines reliability as recovering from failures and continuing to function.
Links reliability to the provider's global spread of datacenters and regions allowing redundant copies.
Defines predictability as covering both performance and cost.
Names a mechanism for each, such as autoscaling or load balancing for performance and estimates, tracking or budget alerts for cost.
States that the benefits depend on design choices and are not automatic.
Notes a tradeoff such as redundancy adding cost, or variable cost being forecastable rather than fixed.

suggested.rationale: This exam objective is conceptual, so reasoning through scenarios that ask which benefit, reliability or predictability, answers a stated outage or budget concern builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: Security and governance in the cloud are about keeping your systems safe and keeping them in line with your organisation's rules. Security means protecting data and services from people who should not reach them. Governance means setting rules about what may be built, where, by whom, and at what cost, then checking those rules are followed. The cloud helps because the provider offers ready-made protective tools and lets you write rules once and apply them everywhere automatically. Think of a large office building: the landlord supplies guards, locks and cameras, while you decide which staff get which keys and which rooms they may use.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company says all customer data must stay inside the European Union. In a cloud with hundreds of engineers creating servers every day, would you rather rely on reminding each engineer of the rule, or on something else? What might that something else be?
lessons.teach:
Security in the cloud means protecting data, applications and accounts from unauthorised access or damage. Governance means defining the rules an organisation's cloud use must follow, enforcing them, and proving they were followed. Compliance is meeting outside requirements, such as laws or industry standards, that say how data must be handled.

The cloud brings three main benefits here. First, built-in protection: the provider runs physical security, network defences against floods of malicious traffic, and encryption (scrambling data so only key holders can read it), so you do not build these from scratch. Second, central, automatic rules: in Azure, a service called Azure Policy lets you write a rule such as "only allow resources in these regions" and have it checked against every new and existing resource. Templates (saved, reusable definitions of a setup) let teams deploy pre-approved, secure configurations every time. Third, visibility: activity logs and compliance reports show who changed what and which resources break the rules, which helps with audits. Providers also publish certifications showing their side meets many common standards, saving you that work.

Worked example. The rule is "customer data stays in the EU." An administrator assigns a policy allowing only EU regions to the company's subscription (a billing and management container for resources). A developer tries to create a database in a US region. Azure checks the request against the policy, finds the region is not allowed, and refuses the deployment. The attempt is logged. A compliance report later shows every database is in an allowed region, which the auditor accepts as evidence.

A common mistake is believing that moving to the cloud makes you secure and compliant automatically. The provider secures its infrastructure, but you still choose who gets access, how data is configured, and which rules apply. If you skip that, a storage area left open to the public internet can leak data even though the provider did everything right. The benefit comes from the tools only when you actually use them.

questions.prompt: A retail company adopts the rule "no storage account may be reachable from the public internet." Here is how it plays out. Step 1: Before any rule existed, the team created four storage accounts, and one of them was left open to the public internet. Step 2: An administrator assigns an Azure Policy rule (a centrally written rule that Azure checks automatically) to the company's subscription, which is the billing and management container holding those accounts. The rule requires public access to be blocked. Step 3: A week later, an engineer tries to create a new storage account open to the public internet. Azure checks the request against the rule and refuses it, and the attempt is logged. Step 4: ??? Step 5: The team closes public access on the flagged account, and the next report shows all accounts following the rule. What belongs in Step 4?
choices: Nothing happens to the older open account, because a policy only applies to resources created after it is assigned.
The older open account is treated as compliant, because the provider already secures its own infrastructure.
The compliance report lists the older open account as breaking the rule, so the team knows exactly which resource to fix.
Azure deletes the older open account immediately, because it breaks the rule.
questions.why: Azure Policy checks existing resources as well as new ones, and compliance reports show which resources break the rule, which is how the team finds the old open account.

questions.prompt: A regional bank moves its customer records to Azure. A national law states how long the records must be kept and where they may be stored. Which term describes the bank's job of meeting that outside requirement?
choices: Encryption
Security
Governance
Compliance
questions.why: Compliance means meeting outside requirements, such as laws or industry standards, about how data must be handled.

questions.prompt: An engineering firm notices that each team builds its test environments differently, and some setups are missing security settings. Management wants every new environment to start from the same pre-approved, secure setup. Which cloud feature fits this need best?
choices: Provider certifications, which show that the provider's side meets common standards
Activity logs, which record who changed what after the environment is built
Templates, which are saved, reusable definitions of a setup that can be deployed the same way every time
Compliance reports, which list resources that break the rules
questions.why: Templates let teams deploy the same pre-approved, secure configuration every time, which fixes inconsistent setups at the start.

questions.prompt: A small design studio moves its files to Azure, assuming the cloud now makes it fully secure. A staff member sets up a file storage area that anyone on the public internet can open, and client drawings leak. The provider's data centres and network defences worked correctly throughout. What best explains the leak?
choices: Storing files in the cloud is never secure, so the studio should not have moved.
The studio needed a provider certification before storing client files.
The provider secures its infrastructure, but the customer still chooses access and configuration, and the studio left the storage open.
The provider failed to encrypt the files, which is the provider's job alone.
questions.why: Moving to the cloud does not make you secure automatically, because the customer still controls who gets access and how data is configured.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, why security and governance get easier in the cloud, using one example of an automatically enforced rule. Then name one limit: what the cloud does not do for you.
lessons.modelAnswer: In the cloud, a lot of baseline security comes ready-made: the provider guards the data centres, defends the network against attacks and offers encryption, so we don't build those ourselves. Governance gets easier because we can write rules once and have them enforced everywhere. For example, with Azure Policy we can say resources may only be created in EU regions; if someone tries to deploy in the US, the request is simply refused and logged. Reusable templates give us secure, pre-approved setups, and compliance reports show which resources break the rules, which helps during audits. The limit is that none of this is automatic for our side. The provider secures its infrastructure, but we still decide who has access, how data is configured and which policies exist. A badly configured storage account can still leak data even on a secure platform.
rubricPoints: Defines security as protecting data and services and governance as setting, enforcing and proving rules.
Names built-in provider protections such as physical security, network defence and encryption.
Explains that rules like Azure Policy are enforced centrally and automatically, blocking non-compliant resources.
Mentions visibility through logs or compliance reports that support audits.
States that the customer still configures access and settings, so cloud use is not automatically secure or compliant.

suggested.rationale: The exam asks learners to match a stated control or compliance requirement to the cloud benefit that meets it, so reasoning through short scenarios like the region-restriction case builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: Manageability in the cloud means how easily you can look after the things you run there. It comes in two flavours. Management of the cloud is what the platform can do for you automatically, such as adding servers when load rises, replacing a failed one, or warning you when something looks wrong. Management in the cloud is the set of tools you use to control it yourself, from a website, a command line, or a program. Think of a modern rental car. It adjusts and warns you on its own, and you still steer it with a few standard controls.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team needs 20 identical test servers every Monday and wants them gone every Friday. What would you want the cloud to let you do so that nobody has to click through 20 setup screens each week?
lessons.teach:
Manageability is the benefit that cloud resources are easy to control and keep healthy. Azure splits it into two ideas.

Management of the cloud covers what the platform does on your behalf once you configure it. It can scale resources up or down automatically, deploy resources from a saved template, replace or recover a failed resource, and monitor health while sending alerts. Monitoring means continuously collecting measurements such as CPU use or error counts. An alert is a rule that notifies someone when a measurement crosses a threshold. A template is a text file that describes the resources you want, such as an Azure Resource Manager template or Bicep file in Azure, so the platform can build them the same way every time.

Management in the cloud covers how you give instructions. You can use the portal, a web interface you click through. You can use a CLI (command-line interface) or PowerShell, where you type commands that can be scripted. You can use an API (application programming interface), which lets other software send requests directly. All of these talk to the same underlying management layer, so they produce the same results.

This works because the provider exposes every resource through standard, automatable interfaces. Building a server becomes a request, not a hardware job.

Here is a worked example. On Monday a script runs one CLI command that deploys a template describing 20 test servers. The platform reads the template and creates all 20 identically. An alert rule emails the team if any server's CPU stays above 90 percent. On Friday a second script deletes the servers. Nobody touched hardware, and every week's environment matches the last one.

A common mistake is to believe manageability means the provider manages everything for you. You still decide the configuration, set the alert thresholds, and own your resources. Another mistake is to rely only on manual portal clicks for repeated work. In a running system that leads to environments that slowly differ from each other, a problem called configuration drift, and that causes bugs which are hard to reproduce.

questions.prompt:
A city library runs a book-reservation app. The IT team needs its staging and production environments to be identical. They also want to be told if the app logs more than 50 errors in a minute. Here is how they use manageability, with one step missing.

Step 1: They write a Bicep file (a template) that describes two web servers and one database, so the platform builds them the same way every time.

Step 2: A PowerShell script deploys that file to staging and then to production. This is management in the cloud, meaning how they give instructions, and because it is scripted the two environments do not drift apart.

Step 3: ???

Step 4: From then on, the platform watches the app and sends notifications without anyone checking by hand. This is management of the cloud, meaning work the platform does for them once they have configured it.

Which choice correctly fills in Step 3?
choices: They ask a staff member to open the portal every hour, read the error count and email the team whenever it looks too high.
They rely on monitoring to collect error counts continuously, and they create an alert rule that emails the on-call person when errors pass 50 per minute.
They add the 50-error limit to the Bicep file so the platform automatically deletes the servers whenever errors exceed it.
They wait for Microsoft to notice the rising errors and fix the app, because in the cloud the provider manages everything for them.
questions.why: Monitoring collects the measurement and an alert rule that the team sets up notifies someone when it crosses the 50-per-minute threshold, which is exactly what Step 4 describes the platform doing on their behalf.

questions.prompt: Azure splits manageability into management of the cloud (what the platform does for you once you configure it) and management in the cloud (how you give it instructions). Which of these is an example of management IN the cloud?
choices: The platform continuously collects memory-use measurements for a database.
An autoscale setting adds two more servers when CPU use climbs during a sale.
The platform automatically replaces a virtual machine that has failed.
A company's own billing software sends an API request to create a storage account.
questions.why: Sending an API request is a way of giving instructions, so it is management in the cloud. The other three are actions the platform performs for you, which is management of the cloud.

questions.prompt: At a sports retailer, an operator changes a server's size in the portal. A developer runs the same change with a CLI command, and an inventory system makes the same change through an API call. What should the team expect?
choices: Only the portal change takes effect, because command-line tools can only read settings, not change them.
The same result each time, because the portal, CLI and API all talk to the same underlying management layer.
Different results, because each tool has its own separate copy of the resource settings.
The API change only lasts until someone next opens the portal, which always overrides it.
questions.why: All of these interfaces send requests to the same management layer, so the same instruction gives the same outcome whichever tool sends it.

questions.prompt: An insurance firm has three regional offices. Over several months, each office set up its test environment by clicking through the portal by hand. A bug now appears in one office's environment but cannot be reproduced in the other two. What is the most likely cause, and what would prevent it?
choices: The provider changed one office's servers without asking. Opening a support ticket every week would prevent it.
Monitoring was missing. Adding a CPU alert rule to each environment would stop the environments from differing.
The portal cannot create identical servers. Switching every office to API calls written by hand would prevent it.
Configuration drift from repeated manual setup. Deploying every environment from one shared template with a script would prevent it.
questions.why: Repeated manual portal work lets environments slowly differ, which is called configuration drift and causes hard-to-reproduce bugs. A template deployed by script builds them the same way every time.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what 'manageability' means as a cloud benefit, using the split between management of the cloud and management in the cloud, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Manageability means the cloud is easy to control and keep healthy, and it has two sides. Management of the cloud is what the platform does for us once we set it up. It can scale automatically, deploy from a template, recover failed resources, and monitor metrics while alerting us when a threshold is crossed. Management in the cloud is how we instruct it, through the web portal, the CLI or PowerShell, or an API. Each of these reaches the same management layer, so we can script and repeat anything. The limit is that automation only follows our configuration. The provider will not choose sensible alert thresholds or correct templates for us. If we keep making one-off changes by clicking in the portal, our environments drift apart and become hard to reproduce. The tooling is powerful, but someone still owns the decisions.
rubricPoints: Defines manageability as how easily cloud resources are controlled and kept healthy.
Describes management of the cloud: automatic scaling, template deployment, recovery, and monitoring with alerts.
Describes management in the cloud: portal, CLI or PowerShell, and APIs reaching the same management layer.
Notes that templates and scripts make deployments repeatable.
Names a limit, such as the customer still owning configuration or manual clicks causing drift.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests whether you can recognise and justify the two sides of manageability in a scenario, and explaining that split back is the core skill.

lessons.plain: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS are three ways to rent computing from a cloud provider. They differ in how much the provider handles for you. Think of a place to live. IaaS is like renting an empty flat: the building is provided, but you furnish it and fix what you bring. PaaS is like a furnished flat: you just move in with your belongings. SaaS is like a hotel room: everything is ready and you simply use it. Each step up means less work for you, and also less freedom to change things.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company wants email for 50 staff. You do not want to install or patch anything, only to add users and use the service. Which option fits: renting a bare virtual computer, renting a platform to run your own code, or renting a finished application?
lessons.teach:
Infrastructure as a service (IaaS) means the provider rents you raw computing building blocks. These include virtual machines (software-defined computers that run on the provider's physical hardware), storage disks, and virtual networks. You install and maintain the operating system (the base software such as Windows or Linux), its patches, the runtime, and your application. An Azure Virtual Machine is the classic example.

Platform as a service (PaaS) means the provider also runs the operating system and the runtime. A runtime is the language environment your code needs, such as .NET or Python. You bring only your application code and data. Azure App Service, a managed web-hosting platform, and Azure SQL Database, a managed database, are examples.

Software as a service (SaaS) means you rent a finished application over the internet, usually paid per user per month. You manage only your own data, user accounts and settings. Microsoft 365 email is an example.

Why this works: each model hands more layers of the computing stack to the provider. You give up control in exchange for less management work.

Worked example: a team needs an online shop, and we trace each layer. Step 1, the physical hardware and data center: the provider handles this in all three models. Step 2, operating system patching: on IaaS the team schedules it, while on PaaS and SaaS the provider does it. Step 3, application code: the team writes it on IaaS and PaaS, but on SaaS (a hosted shop product) it already exists. Step 4, configuration and data: the team always owns these. If the team needs a custom operating system setting, only IaaS allows it. If they just want a working shop quickly, SaaS removes almost all the work.

Common mistake: believing that PaaS or SaaS makes the customer responsible for nothing. You always own your data, who can access it, and how you configure it. In a running system, a PaaS database left open to the internet can still be breached, because the provider's patching does not fix your bad setting.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm wants to host its in-house invoicing app, written in Python, in Azure. It compares renting an Azure Virtual Machine (IaaS) with using Azure App Service (PaaS, a managed web-hosting platform). The layers are traced one by one. Step 1, physical servers and the data center: the provider handles them in both options. Step 2, the Python runtime (the language environment the code needs): on the Virtual Machine, the firm installs and updates it itself; on App Service, ______. Step 3, the invoicing code: the firm writes and deploys it in both options. Step 4, client data and app settings: the firm owns these in both options. Which choice correctly fills the blank in Step 2?
choices: the firm still installs Python, because it chose the language
the provider runs and maintains the runtime for the firm
no runtime is needed, because PaaS runs code without one
the firm installs Python while the provider only patches it
questions.why: In PaaS the provider runs both the operating system and the runtime, so the firm brings only its code and data.

questions.prompt: A charity's staff log in through a web browser to a ready-made donor-tracking application. The charity did not write or install it, pays a fee per staff member each month, and only adds its own donor records and user accounts. Which cloud service model is this?
choices: Software as a service (SaaS)
Platform as a service (PaaS)
A physical data center the charity owns
Infrastructure as a service (IaaS)
questions.why: Renting a finished application over the internet, paid per user per month, where you manage only data, accounts and settings, is SaaS.

questions.prompt: A university research lab must change a low-level operating system setting that its simulation software depends on, and it wants to decide for itself when operating system patches are applied. Which service model meets this requirement?
choices: SaaS, because the lab would only need to manage its own data
IaaS, because the lab installs and maintains the operating system
SaaS, because the vendor tunes the application for each user
PaaS, because the provider manages the operating system for you
questions.why: Only IaaS leaves the operating system in the customer's hands, so it is the only model allowing custom operating system settings and self-scheduled patching.

questions.prompt: A retailer moves its product database to Azure SQL Database, a managed database (PaaS). A contractor configures it to accept connections from any address on the internet, and the data is later stolen. Which statement best explains who was responsible for preventing this?
choices: The provider, because PaaS makes the provider responsible for everything
The retailer, because customers always own their configuration and access
Nobody, because managed databases cannot be reached from the internet
The provider, because its regular patching should have closed the gap
questions.why: Even in PaaS the customer owns data, access and configuration, and the provider's patching does not fix a customer's bad setting.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between IaaS, PaaS and SaaS, using one Azure example for each. Name the tradeoff you accept as you move from IaaS toward SaaS.
lessons.modelAnswer: All three are ways to rent computing, and they differ in which layers the provider manages. With IaaS, such as an Azure Virtual Machine, the provider gives us the hardware, a virtual machine, storage and networking. We install, patch and run the operating system and everything above it. With PaaS, such as Azure App Service or Azure SQL Database, the provider also runs the operating system and the runtime, so we deploy only our code and data. With SaaS, such as Microsoft 365, we use a finished application and manage only our users, settings and data. The tradeoff is control against effort. IaaS lets us customise almost anything but leaves us the most patching and upkeep. SaaS takes away nearly all upkeep but we cannot change how the software works. In every model we still own our data and access settings.
rubricPoints: Defines IaaS as renting virtual machines, storage and networking, where the customer manages the operating system and everything above it.
Defines PaaS as the provider also managing the operating system and runtime, so the customer supplies code and data.
Defines SaaS as a finished application where the customer manages only users, settings and data.
Gives a correct Azure example for each model.
States the tradeoff: more control and more management work at IaaS, less of both at SaaS.
Notes that the customer always remains responsible for its data and access configuration.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine exercises service models directly, and the core skill is clearly explaining who manages which layer in each model.

lessons.plain: Cloud services come in three main types, depending on how much of the work you hand to the provider. With infrastructure as a service (IaaS), you rent raw building blocks like virtual machines and still manage the operating system and software yourself. With platform as a service (PaaS), the provider runs the machines and operating system, and you just bring your application. With software as a service (SaaS), you simply use a finished application, like web email. Think of food: IaaS is renting a kitchen, PaaS is a meal kit delivered with the stove ready, SaaS is eating at a restaurant.
lessons.guessPrompt: A small shop wants email and calendars for its ten staff and has no IT person. Should it rent a virtual machine and install a mail server, or just sign up for a ready-made online email service? Why?
lessons.teach:
The three service types differ in one thing: how much of the stack you manage versus how much the provider manages. The stack runs from physical hardware, through the operating system (OS, the base software like Windows or Linux), the runtime (the language engine your code needs), up to your application and data.

Infrastructure as a service (IaaS) gives you virtual machines (software-defined computers), storage and networks. The provider runs the hardware; you install and patch the OS and everything above it. You get the most control and the most work. In Azure, Azure Virtual Machines is the classic IaaS example.

Platform as a service (PaaS) gives you a managed environment to run your code or database. The provider handles hardware, OS and patching; you manage your app and data. Less control, much less upkeep. Azure App Service (managed web hosting) and Azure SQL Database (a managed database) are PaaS.

Software as a service (SaaS) is a complete application you just use and configure, such as Microsoft 365 email. You manage only your data, users and settings.

The rule for choosing: pick the type that gives the least management that still meets your control requirement. Less management means fewer chances to forget a patch and fewer staff hours.

Worked example: a company has an old app that only runs on a specific OS version with a custom driver. Step 1, does a finished product do this job? No, so not SaaS. Step 2, can it run in a managed platform where you cannot touch the OS? No, it needs that driver. Step 3, so it needs IaaS, where you control the OS. If instead it were a standard web app in a supported language, PaaS would win because nobody has to patch servers.

Common mistake: choosing IaaS by default because it feels familiar. The consequence in a running system is that your team now owns OS updates, security patches and capacity; a missed patch becomes your outage or breach, not the provider's.

questions.prompt: A regional bakery chain's developers built a custom online ordering website in a common, supported programming language. It needs no special operating system (OS) settings or drivers, and the IT team is only two people. They work through the choice step by step. Step 1: Is there a finished product (SaaS) that already does this exact job? No. They want their own custom ordering logic, so SaaS is out. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: Choose PaaS, for example Azure App Service (managed web hosting), so the two-person team never has to patch servers. Which statement correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: Ask whether the provider will also manage the application code. It will, so the team will have nothing at all left to manage.
Ask whether it can run on a managed platform where the team never touches the OS. It can, because it needs no custom OS changes.
Ask whether the team already knows virtual machines well. They do, so IaaS is the safer and more familiar starting point.
Ask whether they want the most control over the OS. They do, because having more control is always the better choice.
questions.why: PaaS fits only once you confirm the app can run without OS access, and this site needs no OS changes, so the least-management option that still meets the control requirement is PaaS.

questions.prompt: A team moves its database to a platform as a service (PaaS) offering such as Azure SQL Database, which is a managed database. Under PaaS, what is the team still responsible for managing?
choices: Installing and patching the operating system under the database
Its own application and the data stored in the database
Nothing beyond user accounts, because PaaS works like a finished app
The physical servers and disks the database runs on
questions.why: In PaaS the provider handles the hardware, the OS and patching, while the customer still manages its own app and data.

questions.prompt: A 40-person architecture firm wants email, calendars and shared documents for its staff. It has no developers and does not want to run or patch any servers. It only wants to add users and adjust settings. Which service type fits best?
choices: Software as a service (SaaS), a complete application they simply use and configure
IaaS with extra storage, because files and email need the most control
Infrastructure as a service (IaaS), virtual machines they set up as their own mail servers
Platform as a service (PaaS), a managed environment where they deploy their own code
questions.why: A finished product already does this job, and SaaS leaves the firm managing only its data, users and settings, which is the least management that meets its needs.

questions.prompt: An online travel agency ran a standard web app, written in a supported language, on Azure Virtual Machines (IaaS) only because the team was used to servers. Months later, an attacker exploited an OS security patch nobody had installed. What best explains what went wrong?
choices: The team chose IaaS by default, so it owned OS patching; PaaS would have handed patching to the provider
The provider failed its duty, because under IaaS the provider patches the guest OS
Nothing about the service type mattered, because every service type puts OS patching on the customer
The app should have been moved to SaaS, where the customer manages its own OS patches
questions.why: With IaaS the customer installs and patches the OS, so choosing it out of familiarity for an app that could run on PaaS made the missed patch the team's breach.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between IaaS, PaaS and SaaS for a new workload, and name the tradeoff you are making as you move from one to the next.
