lessons.modelAnswer: The three types split the work between us and the provider. With IaaS we rent virtual machines and manage the operating system, patches and everything on top. With PaaS the provider runs the machines and OS, and we only deploy our app and manage our data. With SaaS we just use a finished application and manage users and settings. My decision process is to start at SaaS and move down only when a requirement forces it. If a ready-made product does the job, use it. If we need our own code but nothing special about the OS, PaaS. If we need a specific OS, custom drivers or full control, IaaS. The tradeoff is control versus responsibility: each step toward IaaS gives us more control but also more patching, maintenance and risk of mistakes we own. Choosing IaaS out of habit just adds work.
rubricPoints: Defines IaaS, PaaS and SaaS by who manages which layers.
States the tradeoff: more control means more management responsibility.
Gives a decision rule such as preferring the least-managed option that meets requirements.
Names a requirement that forces IaaS, like needing OS-level control.
Gives at least one correct example of each type.

suggested.rationale: The skill is matching a scenario's control and effort requirements to a service type, which is best practised by reasoning through exam-style use cases.

lessons.plain: An Azure region is a chosen spot on the map where Microsoft runs one or more datacenters, buildings full of servers, linked by a fast private network. When you create something in Azure, you usually pick a region, much like choosing which branch of a bank holds your account. Many regions are teamed with a partner region far away in the same part of the world, called a region pair, so one can help if the other has a disaster. Sovereign regions are separate copies of Azure walled off for special customers, such as the US government or customers in China.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a company's app and data live in one city's Azure datacenters and a major flood hits that city, where would you want a backup copy kept, and why not just across the street?
lessons.teach:
A region is a geographic area containing one or more datacenters (buildings of servers, power, and cooling) joined by a low-latency network. You pick a region for most resources, and the choice matters: nearer regions give users faster responses, some services or virtual machine sizes exist only in certain regions, and local laws may require data to stay in a country. A few services are global and need no region, such as Microsoft Entra ID (the identity directory) and Azure DNS (name lookup).

A region pair is two regions in the same geography, usually at least 300 miles (about 480 km) apart, linked for disaster recovery. Distance means one natural disaster or power failure is unlikely to hit both. Pairing brings three behaviours: planned platform updates roll out to one region of the pair at a time; in a wide outage, one region of each pair is prioritised for recovery; and data generally stays inside the same geography for legal and tax reasons. Brazil South is an exception, paired one way with a region in the United States.

Worked example: a retailer in the Netherlands deploys to West Europe, whose pair is North Europe in Ireland. Step one, they configure geo-redundant storage so data copies to North Europe. Step two, Microsoft patches West Europe first, leaving North Europe untouched. Step three, if West Europe fails, the copy in Ireland is used and the data never left Europe.

Common mistake: assuming pairing protects everything automatically. Many services replicate only if you set them up, and some newer regions have no pair at all. Without that setup, an outage in your region means downtime and possible data loss.

Sovereign regions are isolated instances of Azure. Azure Government serves US government agencies and partners, with physically separate datacenters and screened staff. Azure in China is operated by a local company, 21Vianet, rather than by Microsoft directly, to meet Chinese regulations.

questions.prompt:
A dental clinic chain in Japan runs its booking database in the Japan East region. For this question, take it as given that Japan East is paired with Japan West, which is several hundred miles away in the same country. Here is how the pairing helps them, traced step by step.

Step 1: The team turns on geo-redundant backups, so a copy of the booking data is kept in Japan West.
Step 2: (missing) Microsoft schedules a planned platform update for this region pair.
Step 3: A severe storm takes Japan East offline. The clinic restores bookings from the copy in Japan West, and the patient data never leaves Japan.

What happens in Step 2?
choices: The update is skipped entirely for paired regions, because pairing already provides protection.
The clinic's data is moved temporarily to a United States region while the update runs.
The update is applied to both Japan East and Japan West at the same moment, so the pair stays on the same version.
The update is applied to one region of the pair first, and the other region is left untouched until it finishes.
questions.why: Region pairs receive planned platform updates one region at a time, so a faulty update cannot take down both regions together.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes an Azure region pair?
choices: Two datacenter buildings on the same campus that share power and cooling.
Any two regions a customer chooses to deploy to, anywhere in the world.
A global service, such as Azure DNS, that runs in every region at once.
Two regions in the same geography, usually at least 300 miles apart, linked for disaster recovery.
questions.why: A region pair is two regions in the same geography, set far enough apart that one disaster is unlikely to hit both, and linked for disaster recovery.

questions.prompt: A US federal agency's contractor needs cloud hosting in datacenters that are physically separate from the ones ordinary commercial customers use, run by screened staff. Which Azure option fits this requirement?
choices: Use the Azure in China sovereign region operated by 21Vianet.
Use Azure Government, a sovereign region for US government agencies and their partners.
Deploy only global services such as Microsoft Entra ID.
Choose any US commercial region and turn on geo-redundant storage.
questions.why: Azure Government is an isolated sovereign instance of Azure with physically separate datacenters and screened staff, built to serve US government agencies and partners.

questions.prompt: A small analytics startup puts its virtual machines and file storage in one region. They never set up replication, because they assume the region's pair will protect them automatically. The region then suffers a long outage. What is the most likely result?
choices: Downtime and possible data loss, because many services copy data to the paired region only if you configure them to.
No impact, because every resource automatically fails over to the paired region.
The data is automatically moved to a different geography until the outage ends.
Only the global services fail, while the virtual machines keep running in the paired region.
questions.why: Pairing does not protect everything automatically. Without replication configured, and some regions have no pair at all, an outage in your region means downtime and possible data loss.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose a region for a new workload, what a region pair adds, and when a sovereign region is needed. Name one limit of relying on region pairs.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd pick the region closest to our users that offers the services and VM sizes we need and keeps data where the law requires. A region is a geographic area with one or more connected datacenters. Most regions have a pair in the same geography, usually 300+ miles away, so a single disaster rarely hits both. Pairs get updates one region at a time, one region in each pair is prioritised for recovery in a big outage, and data stays within the geography, Brazil South being the exception. The limit: pairing isn't automatic protection. We still have to turn on replication, such as geo-redundant storage, and some newer regions have no pair. Sovereign regions are isolated Azure instances: Azure Government for US agencies, and Azure in China, run by 21Vianet, for Chinese regulatory needs.
rubricPoints: Defines a region as a geographic area with one or more networked datacenters.
Names region choice factors: latency, service availability, and data residency.
Explains that region pairs are in the same geography and far apart for disaster recovery.
Mentions staggered updates, recovery prioritisation, or data staying in geography.
States a limit: replication must often be configured, or some regions lack a pair.
Identifies Azure Government and Azure China (21Vianet) as sovereign, isolated regions.

suggested.rationale: The skill is matching a requirement like disaster recovery, latency, or government data rules to the right region choice, which is best practised by reasoning through exam-style scenarios after reading the facts.

lessons.plain: An availability zone is a physically separate building, or group of buildings, inside one Azure region, with its own power, cooling and network connections. A region that supports zones has at least three of them, close enough to talk to each other quickly but far enough apart that one local disaster, like a fire or power cut, should not hit them all. Think of a hospital that keeps three generators in three different basements: if one floods, the lights stay on. Spreading copies of your application across zones keeps it running when one zone fails.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you run two copies of a website in two separate buildings in the same city instead of in one building, what kind of problem are you protected against, and what kind are you still exposed to?
lessons.teach:
An availability zone is a physically isolated location within an Azure region. A region is a geographic area containing one or more datacenters, which are buildings full of servers. Each zone is made of one or more datacenters with independent power, cooling and networking, so a failure in one zone should not spread to the others. Regions that support zones have a minimum of three. The zones are linked by fast, private, low-latency connections, so copies of an application in different zones can stay in sync.

Why it works: failures like a power outage, a cooling breakdown or a cut network cable usually hit one site. If your workload has copies in separate sites, one copy survives.

Azure services relate to zones in three ways. Zonal services are pinned to a zone you choose, such as a virtual machine (a rented server) placed in zone 1. Zone-redundant services are automatically copied across zones by Azure, such as zone-redundant storage. Non-regional services are not tied to any one zone or region at all.

Worked example: a shop runs its web server on two virtual machines, one in zone 1 and one in zone 2, behind a load balancer (a service that spreads incoming requests across servers). Step 1: both machines answer customers. Step 2: zone 1 loses power. Step 3: the load balancer notices the zone 1 machine stopped responding. Step 4: it sends all requests to zone 2. Customers keep shopping, perhaps a little slower.

Common mistake: deploying several copies but letting them all land in the same zone, or assuming every region has zones. Not all regions do, so check before relying on them.

Tradeoffs: running duplicate resources costs more, and traffic between zones can add a small charge and slight delay. Zones also do not protect against an entire region going down; that needs a second region. Availability zones protect a workload against the failure of one datacenter site within its region.

questions.prompt: A city library is setting up its online book catalogue in an Azure region. The goal is to keep the catalogue running even if one datacenter site fails. Step 1: the team confirms that the chosen region supports availability zones, and it offers zones 1, 2 and 3. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: they put a load balancer in front of the machines, which spreads incoming requests across whichever machines are healthy. Step 4: weeks later, a cut network cable takes zone 2 offline. The load balancer stops sending requests there, and the machines in zone 1 and zone 3 keep serving readers. Which choice correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: Create one virtual machine in zone 2, because Azure automatically copies every virtual machine to the other zones.
Create three virtual machines, placing one in zone 1, one in zone 2 and one in zone 3.
Create three virtual machines and place all of them in zone 1, so they share the same fast local network.
Create three virtual machines in a different region, because zones only provide protection when they are spread across regions.
questions.why: Spreading the virtual machines across separate zones means a failure in zone 2 leaves working copies in zones 1 and 3, which is exactly what Step 4 relies on.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes an Azure availability zone?
choices: A backup copy of your data that Azure keeps in a different country.
A single server rack inside a datacenter that shares power with the racks around it.
A physically isolated location within a region, made of one or more datacenters with their own power, cooling and networking.
A separate geographic area of the world that contains its own set of Azure services.
questions.why: An availability zone sits inside a region and has independent power, cooling and networking, so a failure in one zone should not spread to the others.

questions.prompt: A delivery company wants its stored shipment records to be copied across several zones in its region automatically, without the team choosing a zone for each copy. Which kind of Azure service matches this need?
choices: A zonal service, such as a virtual machine pinned to zone 3.
A single virtual machine placed in whichever zone is cheapest.
A zone-redundant service, such as zone-redundant storage.
A non-regional service, which is not tied to any zone or region.
questions.why: Zone-redundant services are copied across zones by Azure automatically, while zonal services stay in the one zone you pick.

questions.prompt: An insurance firm runs its claims app on virtual machines in zones 1, 2 and 3 of a single Azure region. A large disaster knocks the entire region offline. What is the result, and what would have kept the app running?
choices: The app goes down, but only because the firm should have placed all three machines in the same zone.
The app goes down, because availability zones only protect against one site failing within a region; surviving a whole-region outage needs a copy in a second region.
The app keeps running, because spreading copies across three zones protects against any outage, including a whole region going down.
The app keeps running, because the load balancer automatically moves the virtual machines into the nearest region.
questions.why: Availability zones guard against the failure of one datacenter site inside a region; they do not protect against the entire region failing, which requires a second region.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what an availability zone is and how you would use it to keep an application running, then name one thing zones do not protect against or one cost of using them.
lessons.modelAnswer: An availability zone is a physically separate site inside an Azure region, made of one or more datacenters with its own power, cooling and networking. Regions with zones have at least three, connected by fast private links. To keep an app running, I would put copies of it in different zones, for example one virtual machine in zone 1 and another in zone 2 with a load balancer in front. If zone 1 loses power, the load balancer sends traffic to zone 2. Some services are zonal, meaning I pick the zone; others are zone-redundant, meaning Azure copies them across zones for me. The limit is that zones only cover a failure inside one region; if the whole region is down, I need a second region. Running duplicates also costs more, and not every region offers zones.
rubricPoints: Defines a zone as a physically separate location within one region with independent power, cooling and networking.
States that zone-enabled regions have at least three zones linked by low-latency connections.
Describes spreading copies of a workload across zones so one zone failure does not stop it.
Distinguishes zonal resources from zone-redundant services.
Names a limit: no protection against a full region outage, extra cost, or not all regions support zones.

suggested.rationale: A disaster-recovery planner would let the learner place resources across zones, simulate a zone failure, and see which placement keeps the workload up.

lessons.plain: An Azure datacenter is a real building, owned and run by Microsoft, packed with racks of computers, storage drives and network equipment. It has its own electricity supply, backup generators, cooling and network links, all designed to keep those machines running around the clock. When you rent a virtual machine or store a file in Azure, it ultimately lives on hardware inside one of these buildings. Think of it like a giant, secure warehouse of computers that you never visit. You just ask for space, and Microsoft decides which shelf your work goes on.
lessons.guessPrompt: When you create a virtual machine in Azure, do you think you get to pick the exact building it runs in? Why might a cloud provider not let you choose?
lessons.teach:
An Azure datacenter is a physical facility containing thousands of servers (computers that run workloads for others), storage hardware, and networking gear, supported by its own power, cooling, and network connections. It is the lowest physical layer of Azure: every service you use runs on hardware sitting in some datacenter.

Why this works: concentrating hardware in purpose-built buildings lets Microsoft buy power, cooling, and physical security at enormous scale, and spread customers' work across shared machines efficiently. Each datacenter is engineered so that ordinary failures, like a single server or power feed dying, are absorbed by redundant equipment (spare copies ready to take over).

The key fact for the exam: Microsoft does not let customers choose an individual datacenter. Datacenters are grouped into larger units. A region is a geographic area containing one or more datacenters linked by a fast, low-delay network. Some regions also offer availability zones, which are separate groups of datacenters within a region. Those topics have their own lessons. Here, you only need to know that datacenters are the building blocks underneath them.

Worked example: you create a virtual machine and select the region West Europe. Step one, Azure receives your request. Step two, Azure picks a physical server with free capacity inside one of the datacenters that make up West Europe. Step three, your machine starts on that hardware. You see the region name, never the building.

Common mistake: assuming one datacenter equals one region, or that you can pin a workload to a specific facility. You cannot. If you need protection against a whole building failing, you use the higher-level options built from multiple datacenters, not a datacenter choice.

Consequence for a running system: if every copy of your application sits in a single datacenter and that facility loses power or connectivity entirely, your application goes down with it. A datacenter's internal redundancy protects against small failures, not the loss of the whole building.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm runs its client portal on Azure in the Japan East region. An engineer works through a risk review in three steps. Step 1: If one server's power feed fails, the datacenter's redundant equipment (spare copies ready to take over) absorbs the failure, so the portal stays up. Step 2: A manager asks whether the firm can request one particular building in Japan East that has newer power systems. The engineer's answer is missing. Step 3: Because the firm cannot control which facility holds the portal, every copy could sit in the same building. A full power loss there would take the portal down, so the team plans to use higher-level options built from multiple datacenters. Which answer belongs in Step 2?
choices: No. Customers choose a region, and Azure decides which physical datacenter inside that region runs the workload.
Yes. Japan East is a single datacenter, so choosing the region already means choosing the building.
No. Datacenters do not have their own power supply, so every building in a region has the same power systems.
Yes. The firm enters the building's identifier when it creates the resource, and Azure places the portal there.
questions.why: Azure lets customers select a region but never an individual datacenter, so the firm cannot pin the portal to a specific building.

questions.prompt: A new engineer at a shipping company says, "Our Azure region and our Azure datacenter are the same thing." Which statement correctly describes how they relate?
choices: A region is a geographic area that contains one or more datacenters linked by a fast, low-delay network.
They are two names for the same facility, and the name used depends on the Azure service.
A datacenter is a geographic area that contains several regions linked by a fast network.
A region is a single building, and a datacenter is one rack of servers inside that building.
questions.why: A datacenter is a physical building, and a region groups one or more of those buildings, so the two are not the same thing.

questions.prompt: A ticket-sales website keeps all four copies of its application in one Azure datacenter. During a storm, that whole facility loses its network connections for several hours. What most likely happens to the website?
choices: Only one of the four copies stops, because each copy has its own network connection.
The website goes down, because the datacenter's internal redundancy covers small failures, not the loss of the entire building.
The website stays up, because the datacenter's redundant equipment automatically moves the copies to another region.
The website stays up, because running four copies always protects against any outage.
questions.why: When every copy sits in a single building and that building loses connectivity entirely, the whole application fails with it.

questions.prompt: A hospital's scheduling system runs on Azure. One server inside the datacenter hosting the system suddenly fails, but the system keeps running. Which explanation fits best?
choices: The hospital had pinned the system to a datacenter that guarantees zero server failures.
Datacenters are built with redundant equipment, meaning spare copies ready to take over, so they can absorb ordinary failures like one server dying.
A single server failure always shuts down the datacenter, so the system must have been running somewhere else.
Azure moved the system to a different region as soon as the server failed.
questions.why: Each datacenter is engineered with redundant equipment that handles small failures, such as losing a single server, without stopping the workload.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what an Azure datacenter is and how it relates to what you actually choose when deploying, including one limit of relying on a single datacenter.
lessons.modelAnswer: An Azure datacenter is a physical building Microsoft runs, full of servers, storage and network equipment, with its own power, cooling and connectivity. Everything we deploy in Azure ultimately runs on hardware inside one of them. But we never pick a datacenter directly. We pick a region, which is a geographic area made of one or more datacenters, and Azure decides which physical machine and building our resource lands on. Some regions also group datacenters into availability zones. Each datacenter has redundant parts, so a single failed server or power feed usually doesn't hurt us. The limit is that this only covers small failures: if a whole datacenter loses power or network, anything running only there goes down. To survive that, we have to use options that spread our workload across multiple datacenters rather than trusting one building.
rubricPoints: Defines a datacenter as a physical facility with servers, storage, networking, power and cooling.
States that all Azure services ultimately run on datacenter hardware.
Explains that customers choose a region, not a specific datacenter.
Notes that regions are made up of one or more datacenters.
Names the limit that a single datacenter is a point of failure for whole-building outages.

suggested.rationale: This objective is a foundational fact about Azure's physical layer with no hands-on task, so reading and recalling the definition and its relationship to regions is the most efficient path.

lessons.plain: In Azure, a resource is any single thing you create and pay for: a virtual machine (a rented computer), a storage account (a place to keep files and data), a database, or a virtual network (a private network in the cloud). A resource group is a named folder that holds related resources so you can manage them together. Think of a resource group as a moving box labelled with one project's name. Everything for that project goes in the box. You can label the box, decide who may open it, and when the project ends you can throw the whole box away at once.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you keep a web app, its database, and its storage in one labelled folder in the cloud, and then you delete that folder, what do you think happens to the web app, the database, and the storage?
lessons.teach:
An Azure resource is any individual item you can create, configure, and be billed for. Examples are a virtual machine, a storage account, a database, or a virtual network. A resource group is a logical container, meaning a grouping that exists for management only and has no physical walls, that holds related resources.

The rules are simple. Every resource must belong to exactly one resource group, never zero and never two. Resource groups cannot be nested, so a group cannot sit inside another group. A resource can be moved from one group to another later. A resource group is created in one region, which is a geographic area containing Azure datacenters. That region only says where the group's metadata (the descriptive record of what it contains) is kept. The resources inside can live in other regions.

This works because Azure treats the group as one unit of management. Access permissions, tags (name-value labels such as cost-center=marketing), and policies you apply to a group are inherited by every resource inside it. Deleting a group deletes everything it holds.

Worked example: a team builds a short-lived test of a new online shop. Step 1, they create a resource group named shop-test. Step 2, they create a web app, a database, and a storage account inside it. Step 3, they give the testers access on the group, and all three resources inherit that access. Step 4, the test ends. They delete shop-test, and all three resources and their charges disappear in one action.

The usual guidance is to group resources that share a lifecycle, meaning they are created, updated, and retired together.

Common mistake: putting a long-lived shared resource, such as a production database, in the same group as temporary test items. When someone deletes the test group to clean up, the production database and its data are deleted with it, and the live system breaks. Grouping by lifecycle prevents this kind of outage.

questions.prompt:
A hospital IT team runs a three-week pilot of a patient-scheduling app. Here is their reasoning, with one step missing.

Step 1: They create a resource group named sched-pilot in the West Europe region. They place a virtual machine and a virtual network inside it, and the virtual machine runs in North Europe. This is allowed because the group's region only says where its metadata is kept.

Step 2: They apply the tag project=sched-pilot to the sched-pilot group. Result: ???

Step 3: When the pilot ends, they delete sched-pilot, and the virtual machine and virtual network are removed in that single action.

Which statement correctly completes the result of Step 2?
choices: Only the group itself carries the tag, so each resource must be tagged by hand
The virtual machine and the virtual network both inherit the tag from the group
The tag moves the virtual machine into West Europe to match the group
Only resources created after the tag was applied will carry it
questions.why: Tags applied to a resource group are inherited by every resource inside it, so both resources inherit project=sched-pilot.

questions.prompt: A logistics company is organising its Azure resources. Which of the following arrangements is allowed?
choices: A resource group named apps that sits inside another resource group named company
A database created in the finance group and later moved to the analytics group
One storage account that belongs to both the billing group and the reports group
A virtual machine that belongs to no resource group at all
questions.why: A resource must belong to exactly one group and groups cannot be nested, but a resource can be moved from one group to another later.

questions.prompt: A travel startup creates a resource group in the Australia East region. They now want to create a database inside that group, but the database must run in Japan East. What happens?
choices: It works, because the group's region only decides where the group's metadata is kept
It fails, because every resource must be in the same region as its group
It works only if they first create a second group nested inside the first
It fails, because a resource group can hold only one kind of resource
questions.why: A resource group's region only says where its metadata is stored, so the resources inside can live in other regions.

questions.prompt: A retailer puts its live order database in a resource group together with several virtual machines used for a two-day load test. After the test, an engineer deletes the whole group to clean up. What is the result, and what grouping choice would have prevented it?
choices: Nothing is deleted until each resource is removed one by one; the team should use more tags
The live order database is deleted with the group; it should have been in its own group by lifecycle
The database is moved automatically to another group; the team should nest groups instead
Only the virtual machines are deleted, because databases are protected; no change is needed
questions.why: Deleting a group deletes everything inside it, so long-lived production resources should be grouped separately from short-lived test items that share a different lifecycle.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what an Azure resource and a resource group are, how you would decide which resources go in the same group, and one risk or limit of grouping them.
lessons.modelAnswer: A resource is any single thing we create in Azure and pay for, such as a VM, a storage account, a database, or a virtual network. A resource group is a logical folder for related resources. Each resource sits in exactly one group, groups can't be nested, and resources can be moved between groups later. The group has a region for its metadata, but its resources can run in other regions. Whatever we set on the group, like access permissions, tags, or policies, is inherited by everything inside it. So I'd group things that share a lifecycle, meaning things we create, change, and delete together, such as one app's test environment. The tradeoff is that deleting a group deletes everything in it. If we mix a shared production database into a temporary group, a routine cleanup could wipe it out, so long-lived shared resources belong in their own group.
rubricPoints: A resource is a single manageable, billable item such as a VM, storage account, or database.
A resource group is a logical container, and each resource belongs to exactly one group.
Resource groups cannot be nested, and resources can be moved between groups.
Permissions, tags, and policies set on a group are inherited by its resources.
Group resources by shared lifecycle.
Deleting a group deletes everything inside it, which is a risk if unrelated resources are mixed together.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine has the learner organise Azure resources, and the key skill here is explaining the lifecycle-grouping rule and its deletion risk in their own words.

lessons.plain: An Azure subscription is the container your cloud spending and your permissions are organized around. Every virtual machine, database or storage account you create in Azure must live inside exactly one subscription, and the cost of everything inside it lands on that subscription's bill. Think of it like a separate utility account for each flat in a building: one landlord, but each flat has its own meter, its own bill and its own set of keys. A company can hold many subscriptions to keep teams, projects or test and live work apart.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company wants the finance team to see exactly what the test environment costs, separately from the live customer-facing environment, without adding up items by hand. What is one simple way to arrange things in Azure so the two costs come out separately?
lessons.teach:
An Azure subscription is a logical unit that groups Azure resources (the individual services you create, such as virtual machines or databases) and acts as two boundaries at once. It is a billing boundary: Azure produces a separate invoice and cost report for each subscription. It is also an access control boundary: you can grant people permissions on a whole subscription, so someone allowed into one subscription has no rights in another unless given them separately.

To use Azure you first have an Azure account, which is your sign-in identity. That account is checked by Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft's cloud directory of users. A subscription trusts exactly one Entra directory (called a tenant) to decide who people are, while one account can have access to several subscriptions. Each subscription also has limits, or quotas, on how much of certain things it can hold, such as the number of virtual CPU cores.

Why split work into several subscriptions? To separate environments (test versus live), to give each department its own bill, to keep sensitive workloads behind their own permissions, or to get past a quota.

Worked example: a small firm runs one subscription. Step 1, it notices developers sometimes change live servers by accident. Step 2, it creates a second subscription named Test. Step 3, developers get permissions only on Test; operations staff get permissions on Live. Step 4, at month end Azure issues two cost reports, so finance sees test spending on its own. Accidental changes to live servers stop because developers no longer have rights there.

A common mistake is treating a subscription as the same thing as an account. The account is who you are; the subscription is where resources and bills live. Mixing them up leads to designs where everything sits in one subscription, costs cannot be split cleanly, and a single over-broad permission exposes every workload. Subscriptions themselves can be grouped higher up for shared rules, which is covered in a separate lesson.

questions.prompt:
A charity runs a public fundraising website and a donor-records database in one Azure subscription. Here is how it fixes a problem, with one step missing.

Step 1: An auditor points out that the 12 volunteers who manage the website were given permissions on the whole subscription, so they can also reach the donor-records database.

Step 2: ______

Step 3: Only the two finance staff get permissions on the subscription that now holds the donor records. The volunteers keep permissions only on the subscription that holds the website.

Step 4: At month end Azure issues two separate cost reports, one per subscription. Volunteers can no longer reach donor records because they have no rights in that subscription.

Which action belongs in Step 2?
choices: Ask Azure to raise the subscription's quota so the donor database has more room of its own.
Create a second Azure account for each finance staff member, so that the donor records belong to those accounts.
Give each of the 12 volunteers a new sign-in identity that has fewer rights than their old one.
Create a second subscription and place the donor-records database in it, separate from the website.
questions.why: A subscription is an access control boundary and a billing boundary, so moving the database into its own subscription lets Step 3 limit who can reach it and lets Step 4 produce two separate cost reports.

questions.prompt: An Azure subscription acts as two boundaries at once. Which two?
choices: A network boundary and a storage boundary
A quota boundary and an identity boundary
A sign-in boundary and a directory boundary
A billing boundary and an access control boundary
questions.why: Each subscription gets its own invoice and cost report, and permissions granted on one subscription give no rights in another.

questions.prompt: A game studio's single subscription has reached its limit on virtual CPU cores (the processing units that virtual machines use), and it needs more virtual machines. Based on how subscriptions work, which step addresses this?
choices: Split the studio's monthly invoice into two cost reports
Create an additional subscription, which comes with its own quotas
Create a second Azure account for the studio's lead developer
Create a second Microsoft Entra tenant so the same subscription can trust two directories
questions.why: Quotas apply per subscription, so getting past a quota is one reason to split work into several subscriptions.

questions.prompt: A marketing agency puts the Azure resources of all five of its clients into one subscription. It reasons that every staff member has their own Azure account, so that keeps things separate. What is the likely result?
choices: The agency cannot get a clean separate cost report per client, and one over-broad permission on the subscription exposes every client's resources.
Each staff member can only see resources they created, because the account acts as the access boundary.
Each client automatically gets its own invoice, because invoices follow the accounts that created the resources.
Nothing changes, because an account and a subscription are two names for the same thing.
questions.why: The account is only who you are, while the subscription is where resources and bills live, so one shared subscription means one bill and one shared permission boundary for all five clients.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what an Azure subscription is and why a company might create more than one, including at least one tradeoff or limit of using many subscriptions.
lessons.modelAnswer: A subscription is the container every Azure resource must belong to, and it does two jobs: it is a billing boundary, so each subscription gets its own cost report, and an access boundary, so permissions granted on one subscription don't carry into another. It trusts one Microsoft Entra tenant to identify users, and an account can be given access to several subscriptions. Companies create several to separate test from live, give departments their own bills, isolate sensitive work, or get around per-subscription quotas like vCPU limits. The tradeoff is overhead: each extra subscription is another place to set permissions, watch costs and apply rules, so too many become hard to govern consistently. Also, a subscription is not your account; the account is your identity, the subscription is where resources and charges live.
rubricPoints: States that every resource lives in exactly one subscription.
Identifies the subscription as a billing boundary with its own cost reporting.
Identifies the subscription as an access control boundary for permissions.
Distinguishes an account (identity) from a subscription (resource and billing container).
Gives a reason for multiple subscriptions such as environments, departments or quotas.
Names a tradeoff such as added management overhead or per-subscription limits.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this by describing an organization's billing or access needs and asking how to arrange subscriptions, so reasoning through such scenarios builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: A management group is a folder for Azure subscriptions. A subscription is the account-like container that holds your cloud resources and receives its own bill. Large organisations often have dozens of subscriptions, perhaps one per team or project. Setting the same rules on each one by hand is slow and easy to get wrong. A management group lets you put several subscriptions together and set a rule once, at the folder. Every subscription inside then follows it automatically. Think of a company handbook. Head office writes a rule once, and every branch office follows it, so there is no need to send a separate memo to each branch.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company has twelve Azure subscriptions and a new rule says nothing may ever be created outside European regions. Would you rather apply that rule twelve separate times, or once somewhere above all twelve? What could go wrong with the first approach when a thirteenth subscription appears next month?
lessons.teach:
An Azure management group is a container that sits above subscriptions. You use it to apply governance to many subscriptions at once. Governance means the rules and permissions that keep cloud use under control.

Two kinds of setting are typically applied at a management group. Azure Policy is a rule engine that allows or denies certain configurations, for example "only these regions". Azure role-based access control (RBAC) decides who may do what. These settings work because of inheritance: anything assigned at a level flows down to every level beneath it.

Management groups can be nested to build a tree, up to six levels deep below the top. The top is a single root management group. It exists automatically for each directory, and a directory is the organisation's identity tenant in Microsoft Entra ID. Each subscription or management group has exactly one parent. A directory can hold up to 10,000 management groups.

Here is a worked example. A firm has Sales, HR and Research subscriptions and needs all of them limited to European regions. Step 1: create a management group called Europe-Workloads. Step 2: move the three subscriptions into it. Step 3: assign one region policy to Europe-Workloads. Step 4: the policy flows down to each subscription and to every resource inside them. Step 5: months later, a new Marketing subscription is placed in the group and inherits the rule immediately, with no extra work.

A common mistake is to treat management groups as places that hold virtual machines or storage directly. They do not. They only hold subscriptions and other management groups. Another mistake is to assume a lower level can quietly escape an inherited deny rule. Inherited rules still apply further down.

In a running system, skipping management groups means rules are set subscription by subscription. Over time the subscriptions drift apart, and a forgotten subscription can end up breaking compliance unnoticed. Management groups replace that repeated per-subscription effort with one consistent point of control.

questions.prompt: A hospital network runs three subscriptions: Lab, Billing and Pharmacy. Its security team must be able to read, but not change, everything in all three, and any future subscriptions should get the same treatment. Step 1: create a management group called Clinical. Step 2: move the Lab, Billing and Pharmacy subscriptions under Clinical. Step 3: ____ Step 4: through inheritance, the access flows down to each subscription and to every resource inside them. Step 5: a year later, a new Radiology subscription is placed under Clinical and the security team can read it straight away, with no extra work. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Assign an Azure Policy region rule to Clinical so that only approved locations can be used.
Use Azure role-based access control (RBAC) to give the security team a read-only role on the Clinical management group.
Give the security team a read-only role separately on Lab, on Billing and on Pharmacy.
Move the hospital's virtual machines and storage out of the subscriptions and directly into Clinical.
questions.why: Who may do what is controlled by RBAC, and assigning the role once at the Clinical management group lets it flow down to every current and future subscription beneath it, which is why Step 5 works.

questions.prompt: A retail company is planning its Azure layout. Which items can an Azure management group directly contain?
choices: Subscriptions and other management groups
Microsoft Entra ID directories (identity tenants)
Only Azure Policy rules and RBAC role assignments
Virtual machines, storage accounts and other resources
questions.why: A management group is a container above subscriptions and holds only subscriptions and other management groups, never resources such as virtual machines or storage directly.

questions.prompt: A games studio assigns a deny rule with Azure Policy to a management group called Studios. The rule blocks a very expensive virtual machine size. A team works in a subscription that sits two levels below Studios, inside a nested management group called Mobile. The team tries to create a virtual machine of that blocked size. What happens?
choices: The creation is denied, because the rule assigned at Studios is inherited by every level beneath it.
The creation succeeds, because the Mobile management group sits in between and stops the rule from reaching further down.
The creation is denied only if someone also assigns the same rule again on the team's subscription.
The creation succeeds, because a rule only applies to the level where it is assigned.
questions.why: Settings assigned at a management group flow down through all nested levels, and a lower level cannot quietly escape an inherited deny rule.

questions.prompt: A logistics company has a Finance subscription. An administrator wants to place it under both a Regulated management group and a North-America management group at the same time, so it picks up the rules of both. What is true?
choices: This works only if both management groups sit directly under the root management group.
This is not possible, because each subscription has exactly one parent management group.
This works, and the subscription inherits the rules from both parents.
This works, but only Azure Policy settings are inherited from the second parent, not RBAC.
questions.why: In the management group tree, every subscription and every management group has exactly one parent, so Finance cannot sit under two management groups at once.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we should bother creating management groups when we could just set policies on each subscription. Explain in your own words what a management group is and why it helps, and name at least one limit or tradeoff.
lessons.modelAnswer: A management group is a container above our subscriptions. We put several subscriptions inside it, then assign a policy or an access role once at that level. Through inheritance, every subscription and resource underneath follows it automatically, including subscriptions we add later. That gives us consistency and saves us from repeating work, so a forgotten subscription can't drift out of compliance. It also reflects how the company is organised, for example by department or by region. There are limits, though. Management groups only contain subscriptions and other management groups, never resources directly. The tree can only go six levels deep under the single root group, and each subscription has just one parent, so we have to pick one main way to organise. Inheritance also cuts both ways. A badly chosen deny rule high in the tree hits everything below it, so changes at the top need extra care.
rubricPoints: Defines a management group as a container that holds subscriptions, not resources.
Explains that policies and access assignments made at a management group are inherited by everything below.
Gives the benefit of consistent governance across many subscriptions, including newly added ones.
Mentions a limit such as six levels of depth, a single root, or one parent per subscription.
Notes the tradeoff that a mistake made high in the tree affects everything beneath it.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing management groups over subscription-level or resource-group-level settings in a scenario, so reasoning through situations like the region-rule example builds the right judgment.

lessons.plain: Azure organises everything you create into nested containers, a bit like a filing cabinet. A single thing you create, such as a database or virtual machine, is a resource. Resources sit in a resource group, a folder for things that belong together. Resource groups sit in a subscription, which is the account that gets billed and has its own limits. Subscriptions can be gathered into management groups, which are like drawers holding several accounts. The useful part is that rules and permissions placed on an outer container automatically apply to everything inside it, so you can set something once near the top instead of repeating it on every item.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a company gives a teammate permission to read everything in one billing account, and that account contains three folders of servers. Without any further setup, would you expect the teammate to be able to read the servers in those folders? Why?
lessons.teach:
The Azure hierarchy has four levels, from smallest to largest. A resource is one thing you create and pay for, such as a virtual machine or storage account. A resource group is a logical container for resources that share a lifecycle, meaning they are usually created, managed and deleted together. A subscription is a container for resource groups that acts as a billing boundary (one bill) and an access boundary (its own set of permissions and limits). A management group is a container for subscriptions, and management groups can hold other management groups. At the very top is the root management group, which every subscription in the organisation's directory ultimately sits under.

The nesting rules are strict. Each resource lives in exactly one resource group, each resource group in exactly one subscription, and each subscription in exactly one management group. Resource groups cannot contain other resource groups; only management groups nest.

Why this matters is inheritance. Access permissions (role assignments) and governance rules (policies, which allow or block certain settings) applied at one level flow down to every level beneath it. You manage at the widest sensible level once, instead of repeating work.

Worked example: a company creates a management group called Production. Inside it is a subscription called Retail-Prod. Inside that is a resource group called web-app, holding a virtual machine. An administrator assigns a policy at Production saying resources may only be created in European regions. Step one, the policy applies to Production. Step two, it flows to Retail-Prod. Step three, it flows to web-app. Step four, anyone trying to create a new virtual machine in web-app outside Europe is blocked, even though nobody touched web-app directly.

A common mistake is assuming resource groups can nest like folders, or that a setting on a lower level escapes rules from above. Inherited rules still apply below. In a running system, a too-strict policy set high up can silently block deployments across many subscriptions at once, so place broad rules carefully.

questions.prompt: A university has a management group called Research. Inside it are two subscriptions, Genomics and Physics. Inside Genomics is a resource group called lab-data that holds a storage account. An administrator assigns a policy at Research that blocks any storage account from allowing public internet access. Trace how the rule spreads. Step 1: the policy applies to the Research management group. Step 2: ???. Step 3: through Genomics, it reaches the lab-data resource group. Step 4: anyone who tries to create a publicly accessible storage account in lab-data is blocked, even though nobody set a rule on lab-data itself. Which statement correctly fills Step 2?
choices: It flows down to both the Genomics and Physics subscriptions, because both sit inside Research.
It flows up to the root management group, so the whole directory is covered.
It stays at Research until an administrator assigns it again on each subscription.
It reaches only the Genomics subscription, because Physics has no storage account yet.
questions.why: Policies flow down to every level beneath the one where they are assigned, so both subscriptions under Research inherit the rule whether or not they currently hold a storage account.

questions.prompt: A small design studio wants its Marketing team and its Engineering team to receive separate Azure bills. Each team also needs its own set of permissions and limits. Which level of the Azure hierarchy acts as both a billing boundary and an access boundary?
choices: A resource group
A management group
A subscription
A single resource
questions.why: A subscription is the container that produces one bill and has its own permissions and limits, so giving each team its own subscription separates their billing and access.

questions.prompt: An engineer at a shipping company has a resource group called platform. They want to create a second resource group called shared inside platform so that the two are organised like a folder and a subfolder. What happens?
choices: It works only if platform sits directly under the root management group.
It works, and shared inherits policies from platform.
It is not possible, because resource groups cannot contain other resource groups.
It works, but shared then needs its own subscription for billing.
questions.why: Only management groups can nest; each resource group sits directly in exactly one subscription and cannot hold another resource group.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm assigns a policy on a management group that holds 25 subscriptions. The policy only allows small virtual machine sizes. A data team in one of those subscriptions needs a large virtual machine, so they apply a different setting on their own resource group and try to deploy again. What is the most likely result?
choices: The deployment succeeds, but only in that one resource group, and the other 24 subscriptions stay restricted.
The policy is removed from all 25 subscriptions, because the lower setting conflicts with it.
The deployment is still blocked, because the rule inherited from the management group still applies below it.
The deployment succeeds, because a setting on a lower level overrides rules from above.
questions.why: Rules applied at a higher level flow down to every level beneath it, and a setting on a lower level does not let that level escape them.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how resources, resource groups, subscriptions and management groups fit together, and why setting a rule near the top is both powerful and risky.
lessons.modelAnswer: Think of it as nested containers. A resource, like a virtual machine, always lives in exactly one resource group, which holds things that share a lifecycle. Each resource group lives in one subscription, which is where billing and access boundaries sit. Subscriptions are grouped under management groups, and management groups can nest inside each other up to the root management group. Resource groups never nest. The key behaviour is inheritance: a permission or policy assigned at a higher level flows down to everything beneath it. That is powerful, because one policy on a management group can govern dozens of subscriptions without repeating work. The tradeoff is blast radius: a mistaken or overly strict rule placed high up affects everything below, so a single bad policy can block deployments across many teams at once. Put broad rules high and specific rules low.
rubricPoints: Names the four levels in order: resources, resource groups, subscriptions, management groups.
States that each item belongs to exactly one parent container.
Notes that management groups can nest but resource groups cannot.
Explains that permissions and policies set at a higher level are inherited downward.
Names the tradeoff that a rule set high up affects everything below it.

suggested.rationale: Tracing which inherited policy and permission assignments apply at each scope in an authorization policy evaluator makes the hierarchy and its inheritance concrete.

lessons.plain: Cloud compute means renting processing power to run your software, and Azure offers three main styles. A virtual machine is a whole pretend computer, with its own operating system, that you look after yourself. A container is a lighter package holding just your app and what it needs, sharing the host's operating system. A function is a small piece of code that runs only when something happens, while the cloud handles everything underneath. Think of housing: a VM is renting a whole house, a container is renting a furnished flat in a shared building, and a function is booking a hotel room by the night.
lessons.guessPrompt: A small piece of code needs to resize a photo every time a user uploads one, perhaps a few times an hour. Would you rather keep a whole computer running all day for it, or pay only for the seconds the code actually runs? Why?
lessons.teach:
The three compute types differ in how much you manage versus how much Azure manages. A virtual machine (VM) is software that behaves like a full physical computer. A hypervisor, the layer that splits one physical server into many isolated machines, gives each VM its own operating system (OS), the base software such as Windows or Linux. In Azure this is Azure Virtual Machines. It is infrastructure as a service (IaaS): you get full control, but you patch the OS, install software and pay while it runs, even when idle.

A container packages an app plus its libraries into an image, a ready-to-run template, and runs it in isolation while sharing the host's OS kernel. Because there is no separate OS to boot, containers start in seconds and many fit on one host. Azure Container Instances runs single containers without you managing servers; Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) uses Kubernetes, an orchestrator that schedules, restarts and scales many containers.

A function is event-driven, serverless code: serverless means Azure provisions and scales the servers invisibly. Azure Functions runs your code when a trigger fires, such as an HTTP request, a timer or a new queue message. On the consumption plan you pay per execution, and it scales to zero when idle.

Worked example: a company must run a legacy app needing a custom Windows setting and a specific installed driver. Step one: does it need OS-level control? Yes. Step two: containers share the host kernel and functions hide the OS entirely, so neither fits. Answer: a VM. Now change the need to running code each time a file lands in storage, a few times an hour: event-driven, short and bursty, so Functions.

Common mistake: assuming serverless means no servers exist. Servers exist; you just do not manage them. A related trap is putting long-running work in functions; consumption-plan executions have time limits, so a long job may be cut off mid-task in a running system.

questions.prompt:
A ticket-booking startup has packaged its seat-search service, along with all its libraries, into one ready-to-run template. The service needs no custom OS settings or drivers. It runs all day, and during a big concert on-sale it must add new copies within seconds. Choose the compute type.

Step 1: Does it need OS-level control? No. A VM is not required, and its separate OS would slow down starting new copies.
Step 2: ???
Step 3: The app is already packaged with its libraries, starts in seconds and runs many copies on one host, so containers fit. Azure Kubernetes Service can schedule, restart and scale the copies.

Which statement correctly completes Step 2?
choices: Rule out containers, because they share the host's OS kernel and so cannot run more than one copy on a host.
Rule out Functions, because serverless code runs on no servers at all and cannot handle web traffic.
Rule out Functions, because the service runs continuously rather than in short bursts when a trigger fires, and consumption-plan executions have time limits.
Rule out a VM a second time, because VMs are serverless and cannot be patched.
questions.why: Functions suit short, event-driven bursts, and consumption-plan time limits make them a poor fit for a service that runs all day, which leaves containers.

questions.prompt: A colleague says that Azure Functions is 'serverless,' so the code runs without any servers at all. What does serverless actually mean?
choices: The code runs inside a container that you must schedule and restart yourself with Kubernetes.
Servers still exist, but Azure provisions and scales them for you, so you do not manage them.
No physical hardware is involved, and the code runs entirely inside the user's web browser.
You rent one dedicated VM and patch its operating system yourself.
questions.why: Serverless means the servers are hidden and managed by Azure, not that they are missing.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs about 40 different containers. Each must be automatically restarted if it crashes and scaled out when demand rises. Which Azure service best fits?
choices: Azure Virtual Machines, because each container needs its own full operating system
Azure Container Instances, because it runs single containers without servers
Azure Functions on the consumption plan, because it scales to zero
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), because Kubernetes schedules, restarts and scales many containers
questions.why: AKS uses the Kubernetes orchestrator, which schedules, restarts and scales many containers, while Container Instances is suited to running single containers.

questions.prompt: A media team moves a video-rendering job that takes about two hours into Azure Functions on the consumption plan. What is the most likely problem in the running system?
choices: The execution may hit the consumption plan's time limit and be cut off mid-task.
The function will fail to start because functions cannot be triggered by a timer.
The team will have to patch the operating system underneath the function.
The job will be billed even while the function sits idle, just like a VM.
questions.why: Consumption-plan executions have time limits, so long-running work may be stopped before it finishes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between a virtual machine, a container, and a function for a new workload, and name at least one tradeoff of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by asking how much control the workload needs. If it needs a specific operating system configuration or software installed at OS level, I pick a virtual machine: full control, but I must patch it and I pay while it runs, even idle. If the app can be packaged with its dependencies into an image, a container is lighter: it shares the host's OS kernel, starts in seconds, and moves easily between environments, though running many of them needs an orchestrator like Kubernetes, which adds complexity. If the work is short and triggered by an event, such as an HTTP call, a timer or a queue message, a function is simplest: Azure scales it automatically and on the consumption plan I pay per execution, scaling to zero. The tradeoff is less control, possible cold-start delays and execution time limits, so it is wrong for long-running jobs.
rubricPoints: States that VMs give full OS control but require patching and cost money while idle.
Explains that containers package an app with dependencies and share the host OS kernel, so they start fast.
Describes functions as event-driven serverless code run by triggers and billed per execution.
Ties the choice to how much control versus management the workload needs.
Names a real tradeoff such as time limits on functions or orchestration complexity for containers.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this by giving a workload requirement and asking which compute type fits, so reasoning through scenario-style situations builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: A virtual machine is a computer made of software that runs on someone else's physical hardware; in Azure you rent one and control its operating system as if it were your own server. Azure gives four related choices: a single virtual machine, a scale set (a fleet of identical machines that grows or shrinks with demand), an availability set (a way to spread machines so one hardware fault or maintenance reboot can't take them all down), and Azure Virtual Desktop (Windows desktops hosted in the cloud that people reach from any device). Think of renting one car, a taxi fleet, parking cars in different garages, or lending staff a remote office desk.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you run two copies of your website on two virtual machines, what could still take both down at once if they happen to sit on the same physical rack?
lessons.teach:
Azure Virtual Machines (VMs) are infrastructure as a service: Azure supplies the hardware and virtualization, you choose the size and operating system and you manage everything inside it, including patches. Use one when you need full control, such as running legacy software or a custom server setup.

Virtual Machine Scale Sets let you create and manage a group of identical, load-balanced VMs as one unit. A load balancer is a service that spreads incoming requests across several machines. Scale sets can autoscale, meaning they add VMs when a measure like CPU use rises and remove them when it falls, so you pay for capacity only when you need it.

Availability sets protect VMs inside one datacenter by spreading them across fault domains and update domains. A fault domain is a group of hardware sharing power, cooling and network switch, roughly a rack. An update domain is a group Azure reboots together during planned maintenance; only one update domain is rebooted at a time. Availability sets cost nothing extra beyond the VMs.

Azure Virtual Desktop is a managed desktop and app virtualization service: users connect to a Windows desktop or individual apps running in Azure, and Windows multi-session lets several users share one VM.

Worked example: a shop runs three web VMs in an availability set with three fault domains and five update domains. Azure places VM1, VM2 and VM3 on different racks and different update domains. A power supply fails on rack 2, so VM2 stops, but VM1 and VM3 keep serving. Next week Azure patches hosts, rebooting update domain 1 only, so two VMs remain up.

Common mistake: believing an availability set protects against a whole datacenter failing. It does not; it only spreads machines inside one datacenter. In a running system, a datacenter-wide outage would still stop every VM in the set.

questions.prompt:
A school district runs four app VMs (VM-A, VM-B, VM-C, VM-D) in an availability set configured with two fault domains and four update domains.

Step 1: Azure places VM-A and VM-C in fault domain 0 and VM-B and VM-D in fault domain 1. Each VM is also in its own update domain (VM-A in 0, VM-B in 1, VM-C in 2, VM-D in 3).
Step 2: The network switch shared by the hardware in fault domain 0 fails.
Step 3: ???
Step 4: The switch is repaired. A week later, during planned maintenance, Azure reboots update domain 2 only, so VM-C restarts while the other three stay up.

Which statement correctly completes Step 3?
choices: All four VMs stop, because every VM in an availability set shares the same network switch.
No VMs stop, because an availability set stops hardware faults from affecting its VMs.
Only VM-A stops, because Azure takes down one machine at a time to limit the impact.
VM-A and VM-C stop, while VM-B and VM-D keep serving, because they are in the other fault domain.
questions.why: A fault domain is a group of hardware sharing power, cooling and network switch, so a switch failure in fault domain 0 stops only the VMs placed there (VM-A and VM-C), while the VMs in fault domain 1 keep running.

questions.prompt: An online ticket seller sees traffic jump sharply whenever a big concert goes on sale, then drop back for weeks. They want a group of identical, load-balanced VMs that automatically adds machines when CPU use climbs and removes them when it falls, so they pay for extra capacity only when it is needed. Which Azure option fits?
choices: Azure Virtual Desktop with Windows multi-session
A single, larger Azure Virtual Machine
An availability set spread across several fault domains
Virtual Machine Scale Sets with autoscale
questions.why: Virtual Machine Scale Sets manage identical, load-balanced VMs as one unit and can autoscale, adding or removing VMs based on a measure like CPU use.

questions.prompt: A logistics company has 60 dispatch staff who work from home on personal laptops. Management wants staff to connect to a Windows desktop and line-of-business apps that run in Azure, with several users sharing one VM to keep costs down. Which Azure service matches this requirement?
choices: One Azure Virtual Machine per user, each managed and patched by IT
Azure Virtual Desktop, using Windows multi-session
An availability set, so desktops survive a rack failure
Virtual Machine Scale Sets, so each staff member gets an identical VM
questions.why: Azure Virtual Desktop is a managed desktop and app virtualization service, and Windows multi-session lets several users share one VM.

questions.prompt: An insurance firm places eight VMs in a single availability set in one Azure datacenter. A manager says: "Now we are protected even if the whole datacenter floods." Which statement is accurate?
choices: The manager is wrong: an availability set only spreads VMs across racks and update groups inside one datacenter, so a datacenter-wide outage would still stop all eight VMs.
The manager is right: fault domains are located in separate datacenters, so a flood in one leaves the others running.
The manager is right, but only if the firm pays the extra availability set fee for datacenter protection.
The manager is wrong: availability sets only protect against planned maintenance and do nothing about hardware failures.
questions.why: Availability sets protect VMs only within one datacenter, spreading them across fault domains (roughly racks) and update domains; they do not protect against the entire datacenter failing, and they cost nothing extra beyond the VMs.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between a single Azure VM, a scale set, an availability set and Azure Virtual Desktop, and name one limit of availability sets.
lessons.modelAnswer: A single Azure VM is a rented server where we control the operating system and must patch it ourselves; fine for one-off or legacy workloads. If traffic goes up and down, a Virtual Machine Scale Set gives us identical, load-balanced VMs that autoscale, adding machines under load and removing them when quiet to save money. If our concern is staying up through hardware faults or Azure's planned maintenance, we put VMs in an availability set: Azure spreads them over fault domains, which are racks sharing power and network, and update domains, which are rebooted one at a time. That costs nothing extra. The limit is that it all lives in one datacenter, so a datacenter-wide outage still takes everything down. Azure Virtual Desktop is different: it serves Windows desktops and apps from Azure to users on any device, and multi-session lets many users share one VM.
rubricPoints: Describes a VM as infrastructure as a service with full OS control and patching responsibility.
Explains scale sets as identical load-balanced VMs that autoscale with demand.
Defines fault domains and update domains in an availability set.
States that an availability set does not protect against a whole datacenter failure.
Describes Azure Virtual Desktop as cloud-hosted Windows desktops and apps, including multi-session.

suggested.rationale: The exam skill is matching a stated requirement such as variable load, hardware-fault tolerance or remote desktops to the right VM option, which is best practiced by reasoning through short scenarios.

lessons.plain: A virtual machine (VM) is a computer that runs as software on someone else's hardware. In Azure, a VM is not one single thing. It is a small bundle of separate parts that work together. It needs a size, meaning how much processor power and memory it gets. It needs disks to hold its operating system and data, and a network connection so it can talk to anything. Think of renting a car: you get the car, but the tyres, fuel and parking space are separate items on the bill. Each part of the VM bundle is its own item, and each can cost money.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you rent a computer in the cloud, what pieces besides the processor and memory do you think it would need before it could boot up and be reached over the internet?
lessons.teach:
An Azure virtual machine is a software-defined computer, and creating one means creating several linked resources. A resource is any single manageable item in Azure. The core pieces are listed below.

The size sets how many virtual CPUs, how much memory and what performance level the VM gets. The image is the starting template, such as a Windows Server or Ubuntu installation. Disks provide storage. An OS disk holds the operating system and is always required. Optional data disks hold application data. These are usually managed disks, block storage that Azure looks after for you. A network interface (NIC) is the VM's virtual network card. A NIC must attach to a subnet, which is a slice of a virtual network (VNet), Azure's private network for your resources. A public IP address is optional and makes the VM reachable from the internet. A network security group (NSG) is an optional set of allow and deny rules for traffic. The VM and its parts also sit in a resource group, a container for related resources, and in a region.

Worked example: you create a small Linux web server. First you pick a region and a resource group. Second you choose an Ubuntu image and a size with 2 vCPUs and 4 GB of memory. Third Azure creates an OS disk from that image. Fourth Azure creates a VNet and subnet, or uses ones you already have, and creates a NIC inside that subnet. Fifth you add a public IP and an NSG rule allowing web traffic on port 80. The result is roughly six resources, not one.

Common mistake: assuming that deleting the VM removes everything. Unless you chose to delete the related parts along with the VM, the disks, NIC and public IP can be left behind. In a running account, those orphaned disks and IP addresses keep adding to the bill, and they clutter the resource group.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm needs an internal Windows VM that staff reach only from inside the firm's existing Azure virtual network. It must never be reachable from the internet. First, the admin picks a region and the resource group 'finance-apps'. Second, she chooses a Windows Server image and a size with 4 vCPUs and 16 GB of memory. Third, Azure creates an OS disk from the image, and she adds one 128 GB data disk for the ledger files. Fourth: ________. Fifth, she adds an NSG with a rule that allows remote-desktop traffic only from the office address range, and she deliberately adds no public IP. Which choice correctly fills the fourth step?
choices: Create a NIC and attach it to a subnet in the firm's existing VNet
Let the NSG act as the VM's network card and connect it to the VNet
Skip networking because the VM does not need to be reached from the internet
Attach a public IP straight to the VM so it can connect without a network card
questions.why: Every VM needs a NIC, its virtual network card, and that NIC must attach to a subnet of a VNet. A public IP is optional, so leaving it out is fine, but leaving out the NIC is not.

questions.prompt: A developer is building the cheapest possible test VM and wants to leave out every optional resource. Which resource can she NOT leave out?
choices: A public IP address
A data disk
A network security group
An OS disk
questions.why: The OS disk holds the operating system and is always required. Data disks, public IPs and NSGs are all optional.

questions.prompt: A data team's reporting VM keeps running out of memory and its CPUs are maxed out. The installed software and the stored files are fine. Which part of the VM should they change to get more vCPUs and memory?
choices: The size
The network interface
The image
A data disk
questions.why: The size sets how many virtual CPUs, how much memory and what performance level the VM gets. The image is only the starting template, and disks and NICs handle storage and networking.

questions.prompt: A retail company deleted a VM it no longer needed last month. It did not choose to delete the related parts along with it. This month's bill still shows charges for storage and for an IP address linked to that old server. What is the most likely reason?
choices: The VM's disks and public IP were left behind as separate resources
The image the VM was built from is charged after deletion
The resource group charges a fee for each VM that was ever in it
Azure keeps billing a deleted VM's size until the month ends
questions.why: Deleting a VM does not remove its disks, NIC and public IP unless you choose to delete them too. These orphaned resources keep adding to the bill.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Azure actually creates when someone 'just spins up a VM', and name one limit or tradeoff to watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: A VM in Azure is really a bundle of resources. The VM itself has a size that sets its CPUs and memory, and an image that provides the operating system. It always needs an OS disk, usually a managed disk, and it can have extra data disks. For networking, it needs a network interface that sits in a subnet of a virtual network. A public IP is optional and only needed if the VM must be reached from the internet. A network security group is an optional set of rules that filters traffic. All of this lives in a region and a resource group. The tradeoff is that each piece is billed and managed separately. If you delete only the VM, the disks, NIC and public IP can be left behind and keep costing money. Adding a public IP also exposes the machine, so you need NSG rules to limit who can reach it.
rubricPoints: States that a VM is made of several separate Azure resources, not one.
Names compute size and image as defining the machine's power and operating system.
Names the required OS disk and the optional data disks.
Names the network interface, virtual network and subnet as required for connectivity.
Identifies the public IP and network security group as optional parts.
Notes that leftover disks, NICs or IPs keep costing money after the VM itself is deleted.
