questions.why: The Advisor score is a percentage showing how closely resources follow Advisor's recommendations, so a higher score means more of them have been acted on.

questions.prompt: For six months, Advisor listed Cost recommendations for a logistics firm's three oversized databases, but nobody on the team ever opened Advisor. What happened to those databases?
choices: They stayed oversized and the firm kept paying for unused capacity.
Azure Policy deleted them because they broke Advisor's guidance.
Azure Service Health shut them down and reported an outage.
Advisor resized them automatically after the warnings were ignored.
questions.why: Advisor only recommends, so nothing changes until someone reviews the list and acts, leaving the firm paying for waste.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Azure Advisor does and when they should check it, and name one thing it will not do for them.
lessons.modelAnswer: Azure Advisor is a free service that studies how our Azure resources are set up and how much they are actually used, then gives us tailored suggestions. Those suggestions fall into five categories: reliability, security, performance, cost, and operational excellence. For example, if a virtual machine has been nearly idle for weeks, Advisor will suggest shrinking or removing it and estimate the saving. It also gives an Advisor score, a percentage showing how many of its recommendations we have followed. It is worth checking regularly, especially before budget reviews or after big deployments. The limit is that it only advises. It will not resize anything, block bad configurations, or force anyone to comply. If we need rules enforced, that is Azure Policy. So Advisor only helps if someone reviews the list and acts on it.
rubricPoints: States that Advisor analyses existing resource configuration and usage to give personalised best-practice recommendations.
Names the five categories: reliability, security, performance, cost, and operational excellence.
Mentions the Advisor score as a measure of how many recommendations have been followed.
Gives a concrete example such as resizing or removing an underused virtual machine.
Makes clear that Advisor recommends but does not enforce or automatically fix, unlike Azure Policy.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests telling Advisor apart from Policy, Service Health, and cost tools in short scenarios, so reasoning through situations that ask which tool would surface a given problem adds the most.

lessons.plain: Azure Service Health is Microsoft's way of telling you whether a problem is on their side of the cloud, not yours. Picture a building manager's notice board. One sign in the lobby lists problems affecting the whole city. A note under your door covers your floor: water off Tuesday, a leak near your unit. A light in your kitchen shows whether your own tap works right now. Service Health gives you all three views, from the global picture down to one resource, so you know when to stop debugging your own work and wait for Microsoft.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company's website, running on Azure, suddenly stops responding. Before you dig into your own code, what would you want Microsoft to tell you? Would a public status page shared by every Azure customer in the world be enough? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Azure Service Health is a free set of tools that reports problems and planned work on Microsoft's own cloud platform, filtered to what affects you. It has three layers, from widest to narrowest.

Azure status is a public web page anyone can see. It only lists large incidents affecting many customers or regions. Service Health, the middle layer, is a personalized view inside the Azure portal, Microsoft's web console. It shows only events touching the services and regions (geographic groups of datacenters) your subscriptions use. A subscription is the billing and access container your resources live in. Events come in four types: service issues (outages happening now), planned maintenance, health advisories (changes you may need to act on, such as a feature being retired), and security advisories. You can set Service Health alerts so email or text messages reach your team automatically. Resource Health, the narrowest layer, reports the state of one specific resource, such as a single virtual machine. A virtual machine is a rented computer in the cloud. Resource Health marks it as available, degraded, unavailable, or unknown, and says whether the platform caused the problem.

This works because Microsoft already knows which customers each incident touches, so it can report only what concerns you.

Worked example. At 14:00 your virtual machine in West Europe stops answering. Step 1: open Resource Health for that machine. It shows unavailable, caused by the platform. Step 2: open Service Health. It lists a service issue for virtual machines in West Europe, with progress updates. Step 3: check Azure status. Nothing appears, because the incident is too small to count as global. Step 4: after the fix, Service Health posts a root-cause report you can share with your managers.

A common mistake is checking only the public status page and concluding Azure is fine. Another is confusing Service Health with Azure Monitor, which watches your own applications' metrics. In a running system, that mistake means engineers waste hours chasing a bug that is not in their code. Missed maintenance notices can also mean surprise restarts.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs its order database in the Southeast Asia region. The operations lead wants early warning of planned maintenance and retiring features that could affect the company's own services. Step 1: she rules out the public Azure status page, because it only lists large incidents affecting many customers or regions. Step 2: ______. Step 3: she sets up Service Health alerts so text messages reach the on-call engineer automatically. Step 4: when a notice says a feature the database relies on will be retired, she recognises it as a health advisory and schedules the change. What is Step 2?
choices: She opens Azure Monitor to watch the database's metrics for signs of upcoming Microsoft maintenance.
She checks the Azure status page hourly, since smaller regional events appear there after a delay.
She opens Resource Health for the order database to read its upcoming maintenance and retirement notices.
She opens Service Health in the Azure portal, which shows events only for the services and regions her subscriptions use.
questions.why: Service Health is the personalized portal view that lists planned maintenance and health advisories filtered to the services and regions your subscriptions use, and it is where Service Health alerts are set up.

questions.prompt: A hospital's IT team gets a Service Health notice: an older storage interface their app uses will stop being supported next year, and they will need to switch to a newer one. Which of the four Service Health event types is this?
choices: Service issue
Security advisory
Health advisory
Planned maintenance
questions.why: A health advisory announces a change you may need to act on, such as a feature being retired, rather than a current outage, scheduled maintenance, or a security notice.

questions.prompt: An online bookshop runs three web server virtual machines in Canada Central. One of them is responding slowly, and the engineer wants to know that machine's state and whether the Azure platform caused the problem. Which tool answers this most directly?
choices: Azure status, the public page anyone can see
Service Health, the personalized view of events in your regions
Resource Health, which reports the state of one specific resource
Azure Monitor, which watches your own applications' metrics
questions.why: Resource Health is the narrowest layer: it reports a single resource as available, degraded, unavailable, or unknown, and says whether the platform caused the problem.

questions.prompt: A travel startup's app in Brazil South stops working. The team checks the public Azure status page, sees nothing listed, assumes Azure is fine, and spends three hours searching their own code. Later they learn Microsoft had an incident in that region affecting a limited number of customers. What was their mistake?
choices: They should have opened Resource Health, because it lists incidents across all regions worldwide.
The status page only lists large incidents, so they should have checked Service Health, which shows events affecting their own services and regions.
They should have waited longer, because every incident eventually appears on the public status page.
They should have checked Azure Monitor, because it is the tool that reports outages on Microsoft's platform.
questions.why: The public status page shows only large, widespread incidents, while Service Health shows smaller events filtered to the services and regions your subscriptions use, so it would have revealed the regional issue.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks, "Why bother with Service Health when the public Azure status page exists?" Explain in your own words what each of its three layers shows, and name one thing Service Health will not tell you.
lessons.modelAnswer: Service Health tells us whether Microsoft's platform is causing our problem, and it is tailored to us. The public Azure status page only lists big incidents that hit many customers. A local outage in our region could be missing there. The Service Health view in the portal shows only events for the services and regions our subscriptions use. That includes outages in progress, planned maintenance, health advisories about changes we may need to make, and security advisories. We can also set alerts so the on-call engineer gets notified. Resource Health narrows things to a single resource, like one virtual machine, and says whether the platform made it unavailable. The limit is that it only covers Microsoft's side. If our own code is failing, or our app is slow because of a bad deploy, we need Azure Monitor. For cost or best-practice advice we need Azure Advisor.
rubricPoints: Defines Service Health as reporting Microsoft platform problems that affect your own resources.
Distinguishes the public Azure status page (global, large incidents) from the personalized Service Health view.
Names Resource Health as the per-resource view showing whether a single resource is available and whether the platform caused it.
Mentions the event types (outages, planned maintenance, health and security advisories) or that alerts can notify the team.
States a limit: it does not diagnose problems in your own application, which is Azure Monitor's job.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing Service Health over similar tools like Azure Monitor, Advisor, or the public status page, so reasoning through outage scenarios is the most useful practice, and no current mission or planned engine simulates Azure's platform-health views.

lessons.plain: Azure Monitor is Azure's built-in watching service. It collects numbers and records from your cloud resources and applications, lets you search through them, and can warn you when something looks wrong. Think of it as the dashboard, logbook and alarm system of a car combined. The gauges show speed and temperature right now, the logbook keeps a history you can look back through, and a warning light comes on when the engine overheats. Azure Monitor does the same for virtual machines, databases and web apps.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web app's response time doubles every evening around 7 pm, but nobody notices until customers complain. What three things would you want a monitoring tool to do for you in that situation?
lessons.teach:
Azure Monitor is the umbrella service that gathers, stores, analyses and acts on telemetry, meaning the data a system emits about its own health and behaviour. That data comes in two main forms. Metrics are numbers sampled over time, such as CPU percentage or request count, and they are cheap and fast to chart. Logs are detailed timestamped records, such as an error message or a sign-in event, and they are richer to search.

Log Analytics is the tool inside Azure Monitor for querying logs. Logs are sent to a Log Analytics workspace, which is a storage container for log data, and you search them using Kusto Query Language (KQL), a read-only query language similar in spirit to SQL.

Azure Monitor alerts watch metrics or log query results and react when a condition is met. An alert rule defines the signal, the threshold and how often to check. An action group defines who or what to notify, such as an email, a text message, or a call to an automated runbook or webhook.

Application Insights is the part of Azure Monitor aimed at your own code, a kind of application performance monitoring. It tracks page views, request durations, failed calls, dependencies such as databases, and exceptions inside a running app.

Worked example: a shopping site slows down every evening. Step one, Application Insights shows that the slow requests all call the same database. Step two, a KQL query in Log Analytics finds timeout errors from that database starting at 7 pm. Step three, an alert rule fires when average response time exceeds two seconds for five minutes, and its action group emails the on-call engineer.

A common mistake is confusing Azure Monitor with Azure Service Health. Service Health reports problems with Azure's own platform, while Azure Monitor watches your resources and apps. Picking the wrong one in a running system means your own outage goes unnoticed while you wait for a Microsoft notice that never comes.

questions.prompt: A city library runs a book-reservation web app in Azure. Every Monday morning some reservations fail. The team investigates in three steps. Step one: Application Insights shows a spike in exceptions inside the code that saves reservations. Step two: [missing]. Step three: they create an alert rule that fires when failed requests exceed 20 in ten minutes, and its action group sends a text message to the duty librarian's IT contact. Which choice correctly fills step two, where the team searches detailed, timestamped error records to find exactly when the failures start?
choices: They open an action group and search it for the error records.
They check Azure Service Health to read the timestamped error messages from their app.
They chart the CPU percentage metric, which lists each error message.
They run a KQL query in Log Analytics against the logs in their workspace.
questions.why: Log Analytics is the Azure Monitor tool for searching detailed log records stored in a Log Analytics workspace, and you search them with KQL.

questions.prompt: A logistics company collects two kinds of telemetry from its delivery-tracking servers in Azure Monitor. Which item is a log rather than a metric?
choices: The number of requests per second over the last hour
Average disk read speed charted across a day
Memory usage sampled every minute as a percentage
A timestamped record saying a driver's sign-in failed because of a wrong password
questions.why: Logs are detailed timestamped records such as a sign-in event, while metrics are numbers sampled over time.

questions.prompt: A hotel chain already has an Azure Monitor rule that checks every five minutes whether its booking database's CPU stays above 85 percent. They now want this to send an email to the database team and also call a webhook that starts an automated fix. Which part of Azure Monitor alerts should they configure for this?
choices: A Log Analytics workspace
Application Insights
An action group
The alert rule's threshold
questions.why: An action group defines who or what is notified, such as an email or a webhook call, while the alert rule defines the signal, threshold and check frequency.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm's own invoicing app in Azure starts returning errors after a code change. The firm only watches Azure Service Health for problems. What is the most likely outcome?
choices: The outage goes unnoticed by monitoring, because Service Health reports problems with Azure's own platform, not the firm's app.
Service Health automatically runs a KQL query to find the faulty code.
Service Health alerts the firm within minutes, because it watches every customer's apps.
Application Insights is switched on automatically by Service Health.
questions.why: Service Health covers Azure's own platform issues, so a fault in the firm's own app needs Azure Monitor to be noticed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Azure Monitor, Log Analytics, alerts and Application Insights fit together, and name one limit or tradeoff to keep in mind.
lessons.modelAnswer: Azure Monitor is the overall service that collects telemetry from our Azure resources and apps. It handles two kinds of data: metrics, which are quick numeric time series like CPU usage, and logs, which are detailed event records. Logs go into a Log Analytics workspace, and we search them with KQL queries when we need to investigate. Alerts sit on top of that data. An alert rule checks a metric or a query result against a threshold, and an action group decides who gets told or what automation runs. Application Insights is the piece focused on our own application code, showing request times, failures, exceptions and slow dependencies. One tradeoff is that collecting more logs gives better investigations but costs more to ingest and store. Another limit is that Azure Monitor watches our resources, not Azure's platform health, which is Service Health's job.
rubricPoints: States that Azure Monitor collects and acts on metrics and logs from Azure resources and apps.
Explains that Log Analytics stores logs in a workspace and queries them with KQL.
Describes alerts as rules on a signal and threshold, with action groups for notifications or automation.
Identifies Application Insights as monitoring for application code and performance.
Names a limit or tradeoff, such as log ingestion cost or the difference from Service Health.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests matching a monitoring scenario to the right tool, so reasoning through situations that call for metrics, log queries, alerts or Application Insights builds that skill best.

scenarios.title: Moving a Regional Bakery Chain to the Cloud
scenarios.scenario:
Fernhollow Bakeries is a fictional chain of 40 bakeries. It runs all of its computer systems on servers in a back room at head office. You have just joined the small IT team, and the operations director wants a plan for moving to Microsoft Azure, a public cloud. A public cloud is computing power, storage and software that a provider owns and rents to many customers over the internet.

Fernhollow has four workloads. A workload is one job its computers do.

The first is the payroll database, which holds staff bank details. A regional rule that Fernhollow must follow says this data has to stay on hardware that Fernhollow itself owns and controls.

The second is the online cake-ordering website. It gets around 200 visits a day most of the year, but more than 20,000 a day in the two weeks before major holidays. Today the company keeps extra servers running all year just to survive those two weeks.

The third is an old stock-tracking program a contractor wrote years ago. It only runs on one specific older version of an operating system (the base software that runs a computer, such as Windows or Linux), and it needs custom settings changed inside that operating system.

The fourth is staff email. Fernhollow has no wish to build or run its own email system. It simply wants email that works.

The director asks you for four answers.

1. Which cloud deployment model should Fernhollow use overall: public, private, or hybrid? A deployment model describes where the computing resources live and who owns them. A private cloud is cloud-style computing used by one organisation only, often on its own hardware. A hybrid cloud combines a public cloud with private or on-premises resources (resources in the company's own building) and connects them. Justify your choice using the payroll requirement.

2. For the ordering website, the old stock-tracking program, and staff email, choose a cloud service type for each and explain why. The choices are IaaS (infrastructure as a service: you rent virtual machines, which are software-based computers, and you manage the operating system and everything above it), PaaS (platform as a service: the provider runs the operating system and platform, and you deploy and manage only your application and data), and SaaS (software as a service: you use finished software that the provider runs completely).

3. Explain how consumption-based (pay-as-you-go) pricing, together with scalability, solves the website's holiday problem. Scalability means the ability to add or remove computing capacity as demand changes. Compare this with how Fernhollow pays today.

4. Under the shared responsibility model, which divides security and maintenance duties between the cloud provider and the customer, say who installs operating system security updates for the stock-tracking program in your chosen service type and who does it for the ordering website in its service type. Then name one duty that always stays with Fernhollow, whatever the service type.
subParts: Pick IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS per workload
modelAnswer: Hybrid cloud. The payroll database has to stay on hardware Fernhollow owns and controls, so it cannot move fully into the public cloud. That rules out a public-only model. A private-only model would leave the other workloads without the public cloud's benefits, such as renting extra capacity for holiday peaks. A hybrid cloud keeps payroll on-premises (or in a private cloud) to meet the rule. It moves the ordering website, the stock program and email to Azure, and connects the two sides. A good answer links the choice directly to the data-control requirement and does not just say hybrid is flexible.

Ordering website: PaaS. Fernhollow only needs to deploy and run its own website code and data, and the provider manages the operating system and platform underneath. That cuts maintenance work, and platform services can usually add capacity easily. Old stock-tracking program: IaaS. It needs one specific older operating system version with custom settings changed inside it. Only IaaS gives Fernhollow control of the operating system on its own virtual machine. PaaS and SaaS hide the operating system, so the program could not be configured there. Staff email: SaaS. Fernhollow wants ready-made email and does not want to build or run it, and the provider runs all of it. A common mistake is choosing IaaS for everything "for control". That adds work Fernhollow does not need.

Today Fernhollow buys and runs enough servers for its busiest two weeks. It pays for that peak capacity all year, even though it sits mostly idle at about 200 visits a day. With consumption-based (pay-as-you-go) pricing, Fernhollow pays only for the resources it actually uses during each period. Scalability lets the website add capacity when holiday traffic climbs toward 20,000 visits a day and remove it afterwards. Fernhollow pays more only during the spike and much less the rest of the year. It also no longer needs to buy hardware up front for a rare peak, so it shifts from large upfront spending to ongoing spending matched to demand.

Stock-tracking program on IaaS: Fernhollow installs the operating system security updates, because in IaaS the customer manages the operating system on its virtual machine. Ordering website on PaaS: Microsoft (the provider) installs the operating system updates, because the provider manages the operating system and platform in PaaS. Under every service type (IaaS, PaaS and SaaS), Fernhollow always remains responsible for its own data and information, for its user accounts and who has access (identities and access), and for the devices its staff use. Naming any one of these is correct. The physical datacenter, hardware and network are always the provider's responsibility. A common mistake is assuming the provider patches everything once you are in the cloud. On IaaS, that leaves the virtual machine unpatched and open to attack.

scenarios.title: Fernbrook Logistics moves its tracking app to Azure
scenarios.scenario:
Fernbrook Logistics is a fictional mid-sized shipping company. It is moving its parcel-tracking application from its own server room into Azure, Microsoft's public cloud. You have joined the small cloud team, and your lead has given you four requirements to match with the right Azure building block. A general answer such as 'put it in Azure' is not enough. Each answer must name the specific feature and say briefly why it fits.

Some background terms. An Azure region is a geographic area, such as a part of a country, that contains one or more datacenters. A datacenter is a physical building full of servers, with its own power, cooling, and networking. A virtual machine (VM) is a computer that runs as software on Azure's hardware. You choose its operating system and size, and you manage it much like a physical server. A storage account is a container in Azure that holds your data objects, such as files and blobs. A blob is an unstructured file, such as an image or a PDF. A subscription is the unit Azure uses to bill for resources and to set limits on them. Every resource you create belongs to exactly one subscription.

These are the requirements:

1. The tracking website runs on three VMs in one region. The business says the site must keep running even if an entire datacenter in that region loses power or floods. Which Azure feature should the team use to place the VMs, and why would an availability set alone not meet this requirement?

2. Drivers upload scanned delivery receipts as PDF files. A receipt is read often in its first few weeks and almost never after 90 days. The law requires Fernbrook to keep every receipt for seven years. If an auditor asks for an old receipt, waiting several hours to get it back is acceptable. The data must also survive a disaster that takes out the whole primary region. Which access tier should old receipts move to, and which redundancy option should the storage account use?

3. Office staff sign in to company apps with their work accounts. Security wants an extra verification step, such as a code on a phone, but only when someone signs in from outside the office network. Signing in at the office should stay simple. Which Azure identity feature enforces a rule like this?

4. The finance team must be able to look at every resource in the production subscription, but must not be able to create, change, or delete anything. Using the built-in permission system, what should be assigned, and at what level?
modelAnswer:
Place the VMs across availability zones in the region, for example one VM in each of three zones. A virtual machine scale set (a group of identical VMs that Azure manages together) spread across zones would also work. An availability zone is a physically separate location inside one Azure region. It is made up of one or more datacenters, each with independent power, cooling, and networking. Because each zone is separate, a fire, flood, or power cut in one zone leaves the VMs in the other zones running, and the site stays up.

An availability set alone is not enough. An availability set spreads VMs across separate server racks and update groups inside a single datacenter. That protects against one rack failing or a planned update, but it does not protect against losing the whole building. Common mistake: assuming an availability set gives datacenter-level protection. If the team relied on it and the datacenter went down, every VM would go down together and the tracking site would be offline.

Move receipts older than 90 days to the Archive access tier, and use geo-redundant storage (GRS) for the storage account. An access tier is a setting that trades storage price against how quickly and cheaply data can be read back. The Hot tier suits data used often. The Cool tier suits data read rarely and kept for at least 30 days. The Archive tier is the cheapest place to keep data, but the data is stored offline and must be rehydrated (brought back online) before it can be read, which can take hours. Hours of waiting is acceptable to the auditors, and the receipts must be kept for years, so Archive gives the lowest cost.

Redundancy means Azure keeps extra copies of your data. GRS keeps three copies in the primary region and then copies the data to a second region, normally the paired region hundreds of kilometres away. That means the receipts survive the loss of the whole primary region. Common mistake: choosing locally redundant storage (LRS, three copies inside one datacenter) or zone-redundant storage (ZRS, copies across zones in one region). Neither survives a full regional disaster, so the legally required receipts could be lost.

Use Microsoft Entra Conditional Access. Microsoft Entra ID is Azure's cloud identity service, which stores user accounts and handles sign-ins. Conditional Access is a policy feature in Entra ID that works like an if-then rule. It looks at signals about each sign-in, such as the user's location or network, the device, or the app being opened. Then it decides whether to allow the sign-in, block it, or require something more.

Here the policy would say: if the sign-in comes from outside the office's network addresses, require multifactor authentication (MFA). MFA means proving your identity with two or more different kinds of evidence, such as a password plus a code on your phone. Sign-ins from the office network would need only the normal sign-in. Common mistake: switching MFA on for everyone all the time. That meets the security goal but not the 'keep office sign-in simple' requirement. Conditional Access lets the extra step apply only when the risk is higher.

Assign the built-in Reader role to the finance team's group, at the scope of the production subscription. This uses Azure role-based access control (RBAC), Azure's system for granting permissions. You give a role, which is a named set of allowed actions, to a security principal (a user, group, or application) at a scope (the level where the permission applies). Reader allows viewing everything but changing nothing.

Scope matters because of the Azure hierarchy. Management groups contain subscriptions, subscriptions contain resource groups, and resource groups contain resources. Permissions assigned at one level are inherited by everything below it. Assigning Reader at the subscription therefore covers every resource group and resource in it, including ones created later.

Common mistake: giving the Contributor or Owner role because it seems convenient. Contributor can create, change, and delete resources, and Owner can also grant access to others. With either role, a finance user could accidentally delete production resources, which breaks the read-only requirement. Assigning to a group rather than to each person also keeps access easy to manage when people join or leave.

scenarios.title: Getting Larkspur Freight's new Azure account under control
scenarios.scenario:
Larkspur Freight is a fictional regional delivery company that has just moved its order-tracking system to Azure, Microsoft's cloud platform. You have joined the small operations team. In Azure, a resource is any single thing you create and pay for, such as a virtual machine (a computer rented from Microsoft) or a database. A resource group is a named folder that holds related resources so they can be managed together. A subscription is the billing account all of these resources are charged to. A region is the geographic area, such as West Europe, where Microsoft's data centers physically run your resources.

In your first week, four people bring you a problem.

The finance manager says the monthly Azure bill arrives as one big number. She cannot tell how much the Sales department spent compared with the Warehouse department. She also wants a warning before spending goes over the 4,000 dollar monthly limit, not after.

The compliance officer says customer data must legally stay inside Europe. Last month a developer created a test database in a United States region by mistake. She wants Azure itself to stop this from happening again, not rely on people remembering a rule.

The lead developer is worried about the production database, which is the live database customers depend on. Several people have permission to manage it, and he fears someone could delete it with one wrong click while cleaning up old test resources.

The support lead says that yesterday the tracking website was slow for an hour. Her team spent the whole hour checking their own code. She wants a quick way to find out whether a problem is on Microsoft's side, inside Azure's own platform, in the regions Larkspur uses.

1. Name what the team should use so the finance manager can see spending split by department, and how she can get warned before going over the 4,000 dollar limit.
2. Name the Azure tool that would automatically stop resources being created outside European regions, and describe what it would do when the developer tries again.
3. Name the feature that protects the production database from accidental deletion, and explain what happens when someone tries to delete it.
4. Name the Azure tool the support lead should check during the next slowdown, and say what it would show her.
subParts: Cost by department and early budget warning
Telling whether Azure itself is the problem
modelAnswer: Use tags together with Microsoft Cost Management. A tag is a label made of a name and a value, such as Department = Sales, that you attach to a resource or resource group. Microsoft Cost Management is Azure's built-in tool for viewing, analyzing, and controlling cloud spending. Tagging works because Cost Management can group and filter costs by any tag. So once each resource carries a Department tag, the finance manager can open cost analysis, which is the reporting view inside Cost Management, and see spending per department. Worked example: the order database is tagged Department = Warehouse and the sales website is tagged Department = Sales. Cost analysis grouped by the Department tag then shows two separate totals instead of one. For the early warning, she creates a budget in Cost Management. A budget is a spending limit you set for a time period. She sets 4,000 dollars per month with an alert at, for example, 80 percent, which is 3,200 dollars, so an email arrives before the limit is reached. Common mistake: thinking a budget stops spending. A budget only warns; resources keep running and keep costing money. Another mistake is forgetting to tag new resources. Untagged costs then show up as unassigned, so department totals are incomplete.

Use Azure Policy. Azure Policy is a governance service, meaning a service that controls how resources may be set up. You write rules, called policy definitions, and apply them to a scope, such as a subscription or a resource group. Azure then checks every new or changed resource against those rules. It works because the check happens inside Azure when a resource is created, so it does not depend on people remembering the rule. Here the team would assign an allowed-locations policy that permits only European regions such as West Europe and North Europe. Worked example: the developer tries to create a test database in East US. Azure checks the request against the policy, sees that East US is not allowed, and refuses to create the database, showing an error that names the policy. Azure Policy can also report on existing resources that break the rule, so the database created last month would be listed as non-compliant. Common mistake: assuming the policy automatically deletes or moves resources that already break the rule. A deny rule blocks new violations. Existing ones are reported and must be fixed by the team.

Use a resource lock. A resource lock is a setting you place on a resource, resource group, or subscription that blocks certain actions for everyone, even people who normally have permission to perform them. There are two kinds. A delete lock, shown in Azure as CanNotDelete, lets people read and change the resource but not delete it. A read-only lock blocks both changes and deletion. Here a delete lock on the production database fits, because the team still needs to update it. It works because Azure checks for locks before carrying out a delete, regardless of who is asking. Worked example: someone cleaning up test resources selects the production database and clicks delete. Azure sees the delete lock and refuses, saying the resource is locked. To really delete it, someone with the right permission must first remove the lock on purpose, which is a deliberate extra step. Common mistake: choosing a read-only lock, which would also block normal updates and could break routine work on a live system. Another mistake is thinking permissions alone are enough. Permissions decide who may delete, but a lock protects against mistakes by people who are allowed to.

Use Azure Service Health. Azure Service Health is a free view in the Azure portal, Azure's website for managing resources, that reports problems with Azure's own platform as they affect your subscriptions, services, and regions. It shows three main things. First, service issues, which are current outages or slowdowns. Second, planned maintenance, which is work Microsoft has scheduled. Third, health advisories, which are notices about changes that may need your action. It works because Microsoft publishes this information filtered to the services and regions you actually use, so it is relevant to Larkspur rather than a list of every problem worldwide. Worked example: the tracking site slows down. The support lead opens Service Health and sees an active issue for the database service in West Europe, the region Larkspur uses. She now knows the cause is likely on Microsoft's side and can stop digging through her own code. She can also set up Service Health alerts so the team is told about such issues automatically. Common mistake: using the public Azure status page instead, which shows only broad, widespread outages and may not mention a problem that affects just your region or services.
